utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with my headset. Actually, I don't have a headset. I don't have a problem with my headset; I just don't have a headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, we are Wednesday, the 27th of February, 2008. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Theunens, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. Before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, who has already had an hour and 48 minutes, i.e., he has three hours and 12 minutes left, if I'm not mistaken in my calculations, I would just like to tell you that the Prosecution handed over to us three DVDs on the interview of General Panic. I spent the best part of yesterday, in the afternoon, and this morning to listen to these DVDs. This does amount to quite a number of hours. So these three tapes should be translated and provided in hard copy in the language of the accused, or at least has been said in B/C/S be disclosed to the accused, and if the accused wishes to use that afterwards, we need to have this in English and this needs to be transcribed into English. So check this out with the Registrar and see how you can proceed, but this is the way that we should deal with this matter. Otherwise, Mr. Seselj will have to -- Mr. Seselj has always refused to watch these DVDs. Even if he had accepted, he would have to spend 42 hours watching all these interviews, which accounts for a great deal of time, whereas when you read this in hard copy, it's so much easier. That's all I can say. I tried to address it from different angles, but I believe that the best solution is to provide these interviews in their entirety. Of course, you could select those interviews, but then the accused might say that you've edited the DVD. So to avoid any problem, I think it's better to give him the entire interviews from beginning to end. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I indicated yesterday, we will -- we are prepared to undertake this exercise and make sure that this is transcribed, in particular in light of the way the allegations were being levied -- or potential allegations were being made against the Chamber, if the Chamber were to make any sort of decision as to what parts could be transcribed and not transcribed for the accused. So I think it's a much safer way to proceed this way. I would address two things, though. One, as I mentioned yesterday, the Office of the Prosecutor do not have these transcripts done. We work, ourselves, with the audio and video versions of a number of these interviews. We will be doing this exercise on this particular occasion, but I do need to stress that we will not have the capacity to do this with every single recording or thing that the accused might in the future find it interesting to get. But we appreciate the Chamber's indication to us on this particular point, and we understand the particular importance that the Chamber see in General Panic's suspect interview, and we will do our best to get this done as quickly as possible. And we thank Your Honours for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor now so that you can resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, as you have looked through many relevant legal documents of the SFRY concerning the defence of the country and the role of the armed forces in the defence system, do you agree that everyone in Yugoslavia, including officers, privates and all citizens, were familiar with the basic norms of the International Laws of War as concerns the prohibition of killing prisoners of war and civilians, mistreating people, looting, and everything else that happens in war, but is considered to be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the documents I reviewed, I can conclude that the provisions of International Laws of War, including the Geneva Conventions, and the importance of these provisions was emphasised, for example, in the 1982 All People's Defence Law, as well as in the 1985 Law on the Service in the Armed Forces. There was also particular regulation that applied to the SFRY armed forces, which was the 1988 regulation on the application of the provisions of International Laws of War by the SFRY Armed Forces. I also know that -- and this is specified in the 1982 All People's Defence Law, that the entire population was trained in the doctrine and implementation of the doctrine of All People's Defence Law, but I cannot draw any conclusions as to the extent the population or the SFRY, including the members of the armed forces, were familiar with the provisions -- with these provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you indicate at least one crime which is specified as such by the International Laws of War and is not provided for in the provisions of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia? Is there a single crime not sanctioned by the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Criminal Code of -- the 1990 Criminal Code of the SFRY is included in my report. I'm just checking the date. It's Chapter 16 of the 1990 SFRY Criminal Code, and it can be found on English page 46 of part 1 of the report, and indeed the list includes, as far as I can review it, all the main provisions of the International Laws of War. So page 46, part 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can anyone who has committed a war crime, killed a prisoner, for example, killed a civilian, raped a woman, looted something, or done anything else of that nature, can anyone in such a situation use as an excuse the fact that he didn't know this was prohibited? Can a perpetrator say, "Yes, I did kill a prisoner. I didn't know this was prohibited"? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not a legal expert, but from my own military education, I remember that this cannot count as an excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So anyone -- to conclude from your response, anyone who committed a war crime knew in advance that it was a punishable offence and that he would be held responsible sooner or later, if he was of sound mind, of course. I'm not referring to a madman here, but someone who is mentally in a fit state would know that he had done something punishable; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again just an answer from the common-sense point of view, I think most people who commit crimes are well aware, at the latest afterwards, that they committed a crime, but still crimes are being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that according to the criminal law of Yugoslavia, the offence of not reporting a crime is also punishable as a criminal offence? For example, if somebody sees someone committing a murder, or rape, or looting, and fails to report that person, by that very fact that person becomes an accomplice, the fact that he has not reported it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, this is, for example, also specified in the 1988 regulations on the application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY, which is 65 ter number 51, and more specifically this can be found in Article 21 of this 1988 regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke about the armed forces of Serbia and quoted the relevant provisions of the law -- or rather the Serbian Constitution of 1990. Then the Prosecutor tried to introduce only part of the text of the Constitution into evidence, and I intervened and asked that the entire Constitution be admitted. You know that the Constitution contains Article 135; are you aware of that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm aware of Article 135 and the two paragraphs included in that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Article 135, it says that the rights and obligations which the Republic of Serbia, which is part of Yugoslavia, has under this Constitution and which according to the Federal Constitution are realised in the Federation, shall be realised in compliance with the Federal Constitution. That's what it says in that Constitution, and one of the main obligations and competences of the Federation was defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is indeed the first paragraph of Article 135, but I think that in the context we are discussing it, it is also relevant to include the second paragraph of Article 135 of the Serbian Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please read it, Mr. Theunens, if you have it before you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this other article cannot derogate this one. In 1999 [as interpreted], Serbia enacted a new democratic constitution. It first enacted a new constitution, and then we had multiparty elections. Up to then, we had had the communist system, unlike Croatia and Slovenia, which had elections first and then enacted the constitution. In Serbia, the regime thought it was preferable to first introduce a democratic constitution and then have multiparty elections, and the Constitution was adopted by referendum. That constitutes its democratic legitimacy. And in this Constitution, Serbia had to prepare for all possible outcomes, including the dissolution of Yugoslavia, and it encompassed all the constitutional and legal matters that had to be included. But then it says that the rights and the duties prescribed by the Federal Constitution shall be regulated by the Federal Constitution. Am I right, Mr. Theunens; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before answering the question, on page 6, line 22, it should read "in 1990" instead of "1999", and to answer the question of Mr. Seselj, I am not a legal expert, nor a constitutional expert. All I mentioned earlier was that, indeed, the first paragraph of Article 135 corresponds with what Mr. Seselj said in relation to the prevalence of the Federal Constitution in relation to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. However, the second paragraph of the article also reserves the right for the Republic of Serbia to have its own legislation prevail in case of violation of the SFRY Constitution by another republic or in case of violation of what is called the interests of the Republic of Serbia. And I'm actually -- I'm paraphrasing now. I see that the text of the article is now visible on the screen. But, no, it's actually a different article or a different law we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're wasting a lot of my time with needless matters. You said something about the Federal Constitution and its provisions, according to which a member of the armed forces -- actually, every citizen fighting the enemy with a weapon or some other -- in some other way is a member of the armed forces. We discussed the system of All People's Defence which existed in the former Yugoslavia. In 1991, the country was evidently under threat. There were internal enemies and external enemies; first of all, Germany and the Vatican, and then they were joined by the USA, Great Britain, France, and other countries which wanted to break up Yugoslavia. There were also internal exponents for foreign forces, especially the Vatican and Germany. I'm referring to the leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia. They were conducting a separatist policy. Was it the duty of every citizen of Yugoslavia to participate in the struggle against the internal enemy who was bringing into question territorial integrity and wanted to topple the constitutional order by force; doesn't that follow from the Constitution?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that follows from the Constitution and All People's Defence Law. However, the Constitution and the Law also explain how citizens are to participate in the struggle against external or internal enemies who threaten, among other things, the territorial integrity of the SFRY. And, for example, the emphasis is made on the role of the armed forces, so the way how the armed forces are to operate, their structure, their composition, the things they can do, the things they can't do. All this is regulated by law, and these laws do not foresee the participation of, for example, volunteer units in the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can any law envisage every circumstance that might arise in practice? Is there such a law anywhere in the world which can envisage every possibility that might arise and list it so that whatever happens cannot be illegal? Is there any such law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We get out into areas of speculation and things that the expert cannot answer. The line of questions that have been put have been mainly submissions by the accused. If he wants to spend his cross-examination time that way, I don't really have any objections to that. But this particular one is getting out of bounds, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I didn't intervene because I thought that you were going to sum up your submissions by putting a question to the witness, and the witness would have said either, "I agree," or, "I disagree with you." But your last question involves speculation, so is of no particular interest. It goes without saying that a law cannot provide for all the situations that might occur.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This expert has stated more than once here that he is not an expert on legal matters, and yet he dares carry out a legal analysis of over 200 pages, and his legal analysis is up to the same standard as his expertise as a lawyer, as he doesn't have elementary legal knowledge. He thinks that whatever is not expressly permitted by the law is in fact banned, whereas in fact only what the law expressly bans is banned. How can I teach him that when they didn't teach him that at the military academy? He says it's not provided for by law, for political parties to participate in the formation of armed forces. Well, every citizen can do that under the law. In the spirit of All People's Defence on temporarily occupied territory, it's the duty of every citizen to join in the guerrilla fight, even if there are no units around. If nothing else, they can attack the enemy in the street or pour poison in their coffee. So I oppose the objection by the Prosecutor, because it's unjustified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the country found itself in a state of crisis with a strong internal enemy supported by foreign forces, was it under the Constitution the duty of every subject, including every political party, to participate in every possible way in the defence of the territorial integrity and constitutional order of the country? Was this the duty of every political party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The question has been asked and answered, and the witness is not accepting the answer he has been given, which is, yes, but provided that certain steps were taken at the highest level of the state in order to make these citizens act lawfully when they engaged in combat. This has been said two or three times already by the expert, and the answer is just not being accepted. We should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If it's rejected, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed. The question has already been asked on several occasions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated more than once, when asked by the members of the Trial Chamber during your examination-in-chief, and also in your testimony in other cases, you said that you did not deal with the military organisation of the other side, the opposing side, the Croatian separatists, the Muslim separatists and so on; isn't that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the way the question is asked is a bit misleading. In the other cases, in the other trials, I had to testify or I was requested to prepare an expert report, the tasking was always that I had to address the role of a particular group, and this happened to be always -- for the Milosevic trial, it was the SFRY armed forces. In the Martic trial, it was the forces of the SCO Krajina and subsequently the RSK; and in the Vukovar trial, it was the Gas Motorised Brigade. I was asked to address the role of these organisations, and when carrying out that task, I considered it not necessary to address the role of any other parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How is it possible, Mr. Theunens, for you to represent correctly, objectively and impartially the overall military organisation of Yugoslavia, of the Serbian people, covering -- without covering in your analysis what happened on that plane -- what happened in that domain on the opposing side? Why didn't you say the paramilitary formations appeared first in Slovenia, then in Croatia, and only then among the Serbs; isn't that essential for your expertise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an important question I have wanted to put to you. I'm impatient to know what your answer is going to be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my report is not intended as a conflict analysis. It analyses the role of one particular party in the conflict. Now, I didn't -- or I don't consider it necessary, when analysing the role of one party and the way how that party operated its internal structure, the composition of that party, the relation of the various components within that party with the other aspects of the structure as well as with outside organisations or individuals, that in that context there is the requirement to also address what the other parties in the conflict may have done. It's not a question of looking at action-reaction, and so on and so on. It's just a question of looking at one party, in this particular case the SRS/SCP volunteers, and how they interacted with the SFRY armed forces, i.e., the JNA, and what remained of the TO of Croatia, I mean by that the self-established local Serb TO, as well as other forces like the VRS and the SVK. There is no need -- there was no need to explain or to talk about ZNG or HDZ forces or MUP or the Slovene TO in order to address or to understand what SRS volunteers were doing in the conflict and how they interacted with the JNA but also with the SRS war staff. That would be another subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, a few days ago you showed us on a map where the JNA was positioned in Croatia, and if I remember correctly, you indicated three positions on the map which, according to you, were where the Serbs were located in Croatia, and this is what you had explained to us. You said that they had been redeployed because there were Serbs in that part of the country. This is how you saw things. But when you provided this answer, I was asking myself whether these positions could not be due to another fact, i.e., the presence of the Croatia Army in these areas, and that in that case, if the expert only looks into the ethnic composition to understand that the JNA's position there, without addressing the other forces and without addressing the positions of the other forces, there's something missing. So this is a question that's now been put to you by the accused, which is the question I have for you also. Why, in your study, did you not look into the situation of the other side to draw comparisons thereof and to draw conclusions thereof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map, which is visible now on the screen, is actually a graphic representation of what Borisav Jovic, who was the outgoing chairman of the SFRY Presidency, and Slobodan Milosevic, on the 5th of July, 1991, discussed with General Kadijevic. Jovic does not address the role of the Croats. Jovic just says that the JNA has to be concentrated along a line with a western limit, an eastern limit and a southern limit, in order to have the JNA concentrated in areas with a Serb presence. Jovic doesn't talk about the Croats, so the map as I drew it in the courtroom is only a representation of what Jovic says. It doesn't address the behaviour or the activities of the force on the Croatian side. It is clear that the end state, as it is explained by Kadijevic in his book, when he talks about the situation that exists at the end of what he calls the second stage of the second phase, when he says that all Serb areas have been liberated, with the exception of a part of Western Slavonia and so on and so on, it is clear that this end state is the result of a conflict where two parties are involved. But it was not my ambition to analyse the entire conflict. I only addressed Kadijevic's book -- or I used Kadijevic's book in connection with contemporaneous documents, the letter by Kadijevic or the order by Kadijevic and the letter by Adzic before 1991 to show how the mission of the JNA had been changed. That is the only goal I pursued, which is, I think, a very modest goal, and is far less ambitious than really analysing the entire conflict, because in that case obviously I would also have addressed the role of the Croatian forces, their organisation and their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, had you ever dealt with scientific or scholarly work, you would know that not a single social, political or military problem can be successfully viewed without looking at the historical context and that all phenomena in society have a cause-and-effect relationship. Now, your alleged research you directed in just one direction, towards one segment, you just looked at one side, and it is impossible to understand the cause and effect and to take in the entire historical context; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've tried to explain, this report is not about cause and effect. This report is about the role of a particular group and the relations that particular group had with particular individuals. And, I mean, looking back at my education and just -- just looking at my bookshelf at home, there are plenty of books and studies from various scientific level where it is perfectly possible that -- or which study only one party that participate in a conflict. There may be, for example, an analysis about the -- I don't know, the conflict in Vietnam, which obviously will talk about the two parties, but there are also plenty of studies on the organisation, structure and the role of the Viet Cong, as well as there are different studies, books, on the role, organisation, failures and so on of the US Armed Forces, and I would see this report in the same context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, whilst listening to you, I was thinking of a video we saw not with you here but with other witnesses, and in that video we see a young woman who is leaving Belgrade to go to Vukovar, and she explains why she is going. If you like, we could watch that video again, and when you do so, a lot of questions come to your mind. Does this lady go to Vukovar because she's heard speeches of Mr. Seselj and that's why she's going, or is she going to Vukovar because she is a member of the SRS and she's received political instructions, or is it the case that, as a simple citizen, an ordinary citizen of Serbia, she thinks that she will defend her homeland by going to Vukovar, or is she going there because of what happened to her family during the Second World War, and so on and so forth. A lot of questions can be asked about the behaviour of this, quote/unquote, "fighter," but if you look at her participation in the struggle only through the perspective of affiliation to the SRS, then this might be a restricted interpretation of a participation in the struggle, and that's what scientific approach is all about. You have to examine all possibilities before reaching a conclusion with a certain level of certainty, because if you only look at one side of a problem, without addressing the others, then you risk making a mistake. So what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in part 1 of the report, there is a section number 3 which deals with Serbian volunteers and paramilitaries in general terms. It's correct that I have not addressed -- or I have not studied the particular motivation various volunteers may have had to participate in the conflict. I think that would be outside my field of expertise because it would be first and foremost, in my view, a study in psychology and a use of propaganda, and when I say "psychology," group psychology, which is obviously outside my field of expertise. I think that the information I have included and the documents I have reviewed in this section 3 of part 1 of the report is sufficient to understand the development of the issue of volunteers and how it was handled by the authorities in the Republic of Serbia, especially during the latter half of 1991. In part 2 of the report, in section 2, I do limit myself to SRS volunteers -- SRS and SCP volunteers, but again I have not attempted to make an inventory in order to determine why somebody, whoever, somebody from Serbia or maybe somebody who came back -- a Serb immigrant who came back from, I don't know, Germany or Canada, wherever, why that person decided to join the conflict, but I limited myself to studying and analysing how the SRS organised, trained or participated in the training, participated in the finance, dispatched, and so on the volunteers which were affiliated to it. And I would really like to emphasise the importance, for example, of the articles I include in the report, articles published in the magazine "Velika Serbia," which is the SRS party magazine, because these articles show very well what the motivation -- what the driving factor is for volunteers who join the SRS, to participate in the conflict, and which ideology they were implementing while participating in the conflict. So the report only studies one particular group of volunteers, and they were in the conflict, and these volunteers are volunteers from which, from studying the documents, it is that they are affiliated with the SRS/SCP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you weren't ready to look at the cause-and-effect relationship and the circumstances which forced the Serb population in the Slovenian villages to seek volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, because where would the Serbian Radical Party be able to send its volunteers if those volunteers weren't something that the people of those places desired to have among them? Now tell me this, please: All Serb fighters in this war who said of themselves that they were Chetniks, were they necessarily volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, they were not, but I think when you look at my report, from the references I use, from the sources, it is obvious that there these statements like "Chetniks" and so on are not statements they make without any factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But here in your report, you introduced documents in which Chetniks are mentioned, and there are no indices that those Chetniks were in fact volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if Mr. Seselj would give me -- would show me a specific document or would give a reference for a document, we could discuss it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you had that report by the officer, the security officer of the Guards Brigade reporting to the Federal Secretariat in Belgrade. You presented that here, and he said that the Chetniks killed prisoners of war in some places. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I remember that document, but in the same paragraph the drafter of the document also makes reference to Mr. Seselj and the speeches of Mr. Seselj. So I think we can conclude from that that the drafter knows very well what he wants to say when he used the term "Chetnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that same document, the author sets out the problems, how he sees them, what he sees as being problems, and then he lists them. And among others, he lists my speeches, and some Chetniks, and some other problems. He puts that all in one heap. But where is there an indicator that those Chetniks were, in fact, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party? You can see that the author is ideologically coloured, that he was probably a communist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, can you give us the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have it here somewhere. I've set it aside. But I don't want to waste too much time. That's my biggest fear. It's a document that was already presented here in court and signed by Lieutenant Colonel Dragoljub Dakic, I assume -- Dukic, Dukic. It's a document under number 649. But, you know, I don't want to go into that. I'd just like to discuss the problem, rather than looking at paper, because we lose a lot of time looking at paper. But, anyway, it's on the second page of that particular document, and this lieutenant colonel enumerates what is being tolerated unjustly. He says nationalistic ideological symbols, songs, speeches of Vojislav Seselj, the liquidation of prisoners of war by the Chetniks, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Sir, you see there before you a communist officer who doesn't like anything that's nationalistic, and then in his report, he introduces alleged cases of liquidation of prisoners of war, but he doesn't say who, what, where, who liquidated them. A security officer must file a criminal report straightaway. There was no criminal report. Did you ever wonder why there was no criminal report, whereas the lieutenant colonel says that's what happened too? This happened before the fall of Vukovar; isn't that right? This is a report sent out before the fall of Vukovar, is that correct, on the 7th of November, 1991, in fact; isn't that right, Mr. Theunens? Did you ever wonder, did you ask yourself why there are no detail, detailed information there? Did this communist think the whole thing up, imagine the whole thing about the liquidation of prisoners of war? And if there had been liquidations, then he must have said, "So-and-so prisoners were liquidated by so-and-so. I filed a criminal report with the authorities, the District Court." There's none of that, nothing, just a bare assertion which is not commensurate to what a lieutenant colonel should be doing. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from this particular document we cannot conclude whether a criminal report was filed or not, and if it was filed, by whom. In the course of the investigation of -- for the Vukovar case, numerous requests for assistance were sent to the Republic of Serbia-Montenegro and subsequently to the Republic of Serbia to ask them for reports, including criminal reports, on crimes that had happened or allegedly happened during the operations in Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, but we rarely received a particular response. This document, for example, was only received by the OTP after March 2006, because that's why this particular document, 65 ter number 649, is included in the addendum to the report. And I think to conclude my reply, it's important to note that Mr. Seselj characterizes the chief of security at the Cabinet of the SSNO as a communist officer who doesn't like nationalists, because I think that summarises very well the problem we were seeing within the armed forces at that stage, where recruits or conscripts do not want to serve in the JNA, i.e., in the legal armed forces because they consider the JNA a communist army, and therefore prefer to serve in party-controlled volunteer units who follow or who adhere to an ideology which is, as Mr. Seselj calls it, characterized or known as nationalistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mr. Theunens, that one of the reasons for the unsuccessful mobilisation was that people didn't want to wear the five-pointed red star, isn't that right, as a communist insignia; wasn't that one of the reasons for which the mobilisation proved unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, but it's not just the symbol that counts, it is everything that's behind that symbol. The five-pointed red star became a symbol of something which was not appreciated or which was actually rejected -- I correct myself, which was rejected by these volunteers who prefer to serve in party-affiliated volunteer groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it the communist officers who were the problem, who were members of the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia? Can you quote an example anywhere in the world where an army formed its political party, and a communist one at that? When the League of Communists disintegrated, the committee of the League of Communists within the JNA made the decision for them to form their own political party, and that party went to the elections in 1990 and was unsuccessful. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard about the establishment of a party called -- I'm not sure about the name, but it had the name -- it included also the Party for Yugoslavia, and indeed there were efforts done in the armed forces to include as many senior officers as possible. But otherwise, communism was not introduced in 1990. Tito's vision of communism existed throughout or applied throughout the existence of the SFRY, and hence the defence doctrine of All People's Defence which was introduced in 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the problem we have here on the Bench is that we have already started this trial for quite some time and we haven't heard any witnesses who were also volunteers and could have told us how everything worked. That's a handicap for us. In a way, you come too early, considering evidence we could have heard if volunteers had testified before you. Having said that, the question put to you by Mr. Seselj may be significant for the future. The accused is asking you the following: Apparently these volunteers wanted to serve in the armed forces, in general, but they were hostile to the JNA, represented by the five-pointed stars and whose officers were former communist officers, and basically the JNA was the representative of a system that was in the process of changing. There was some lack of confidence in the JNA, and these so-called volunteers wanted to stick together, and they didn't have any military training. Then that might explain some of the problems that occurred later on. But apparently this occurred because -- or as a reaction against the JNA and maybe not because of anything related to a greater Serbia. When these witnesses come and testify, we'll ask them, we'll ask them why they became volunteers. But as far as you're concerned, although in your report you only studied part of -- parts of the issues, based on the conclusions of your report, can you tell us whether these volunteers joined because of a greater Serbia or did they join because they wanted to defend their nation, their homeland? And did they decide to form groups of volunteers because they -- as a sort of reaction against the JNA that was representative for the past? Can you please give me an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the problem arises when you use the term "greater Serbia" and then you ask, "Or did they join because they wanted to defend their nation?" The question is, what is their nation, because the JNA stood for all the nations and nationalities in Yugoslavia, as did the SFRY armed forces, whereas based on the documents I reviewed while preparing this report, volunteers who joined groups affiliated to the SRS/SCP were driven by Serb nationalism. At least that is what I can conclude from, for example, the interviews that are -- or the articles published in "Velika Serbia," the party magazine of the SRS, where, for example, Vojvodas or other volunteers are interviewed, and they all talk about the requirement to protect the Serbs, the threats by the Ustashas and the Turks, I mean these are derogatory terms, and so on. They don't talk about the requirement to defend Yugoslavia, so that is the problem. Instead of wanting to fight into the multi-ethnic JNA, even though that multi-ethnicity was changing over time, they prefer to fight for a particular cause, which is the Serbian cause. And they feel that, at least in the beginning, the JNA is not serving that cause well, and therefore they choose to fight in their own groups, and the cause being the Serbian cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, isn't it obvious that the Serbs were under threat with Tudjman's rule and that that was the reason for the volunteers from Serbia to come to the rescue before the JNA was involved in the conflict at all? What happened first, let's look at that, the armed conflict between the JNA and Tudjman's paramilitary formations, or the conflict between bare-handed Serb people who didn't want to subjugate themselves to Tudjman's paramilitary formations and asked for the assistance of volunteers from Serbia? Which?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a question where, depending on the source, there are different answers. It's obvious that when you ask a Serbian source or when you consult a Serbian source, you will get a completely different reply than when you consult a Croatian source. My understanding, from comparing the different sources, is that actually the Serbs in Croatia, when they felt that Croatia was becoming independent and when they saw that the HDZ was gaining influence, they started to arm themselves, for example, in the Krajina; and, for example, they took control of certain police stations or they said that, "We don't accept Croatian symbols anymore," independent of whether Tudjman was already elected as a president. It is correct also that the statements, the public statements Tudjman made, were not very helpful to increase the confidence of the Serbs to live in an independent Croatia. That's one of the problems, the use of the media on both sides, where media in Serbia increased ethnical fears, and actually the authorities in Croatia did nothing to calm down these fears or to provide trust to the Serbs who felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of an expert are you if you don't know that the official name of the general's party is the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia? So, in fact, you didn't deal with the role of that party at all in the armed forces and in the war, isn't that right, because you don't even know the official name?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember the name of the party now, but I have not seen, when studying -- I mean, when looking at the documents I included in the report, and other documents, I have not come across information that convinced me of including information on the League of Communists Party for Yugoslavia into my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You here sent the OTP -- and when I said "you," you are the Prosecution, because not much difference between you and Mr. Marcussen. The document is under number 604, 604. It's a confidential document signed by Lieutenant Colonel Milan Eremija sent to the Command of the military District -- or rather the 1st Military District. And he mentions there problems in the village of Lovas or the killing of prisoners because they were forced to go into the minefields and clear up the minefields with their own bodies, physically, and he is asking for the disarming of the paramilitaries, especially the Dusan Silni, Chetniks, and Arkan's men, Arkan's soldiers, and that organs of authority that should be included into that action, and the organs of the Republic of Serbia. It is a document of the 23rd of October. So there is some certain -- some Chetniks who weren't in the JNA, is that correct, on the 23rd of October, 1991? Can we see from this that there were Chetniks who were not in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, Your Honours. He doesn't -- Eremija doesn't state that -- I mean, he uses the term "paramilitaries," but it's not clear whether these Chetniks or other paramilitaries are part of the JNA or the local Serb TO or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had you studied that, you would know that the JNA wasn't in the village of Lovas at all, but you weren't interested in that. Now, why would he ask for the disarmament of a part of the JNA, why would he do that, when we definitely asserted that at the end of October, all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Slovenia were in the JNA? After September, we didn't have any volunteers anywhere outside the JNA, and you agreed with that, did you not? So these Chetniks mentioned here by Eremija cannot be volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; am I right there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are several questions included in this question. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There's a problem, in my view, with the question, because it presupposes that the premise for the question is correct, namely, that there was no JNA in the area. Now, I don't want to make submissions on this because I don't want to influence the witness's answer, but I just want to point this out on the record. Then we can deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand where your objection lies, Mr. Marcussen. I really don't understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if I understand correctly, you're saying that in that particular area, there was no JNA, so you are certain of it, apparently. That's the premise you use, there's no JNA there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 2, for example, of the report, the penultimate paragraph, Lieutenant Colonel Eremija says that in the village of Lovas, there was the Territorial Defence of Lovas and the Dusan Silni Detachment. That's what Lieutenant Colonel Eremija says. And I claim there were no volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there even if a JNA soldier happened to lose his way and find himself there, because I know exactly where the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to documents I reviewed, Lovas was located in the zone of responsibility of the unit of Colonel -- of Lieutenant Colonel Milan Eremija, i.e., the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division. Whether at the time of the crime in Lovas there was a physical presence of members of that unit in Lovas, we cannot establish from this document. In order to reply also to the previous questions of Mr. Seselj, I know from documents and other information related to the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar that at times they removed volunteers from their zone of responsibility even when these volunteers were subordinated to the Guards Motorised Brigade, because in one case they discovered that the volunteers were not behaving well, and the Guards Motorised Brigade decided, "Well, we get rid of that." And there's, for example, information that members of the anti-terrorist unit of the Guards Motorised Brigade were involved in disarming a small group of volunteers and kicking them out of the area. I'm not able to see the other questions that were included in the previous question of Mr. Seselj, but, anyway, Eremija states about the role of the Dusan Silni Detachment, as well as Tiolovac [phoen], in the crime in Lovas. He doesn't mention Chetniks in that particular context of the crime in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, there were two groups of volunteers that the 1st Guards Brigade removed from Vukovar, although they had previously been under its command, but those groups were not volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. Did you find anywhere information showing that these were members of the SRS, the ones removed for indiscipline? Have you found that information anywhere?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but I didn't -- unless something went wrong with the translation, but I didn't claim that they were volunteers of the Radical Party that were removed by the Guards Motorised Brigade. I don't remember the affiliation of these volunteers that were removed by the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You ignored a very important source from which you could have been able to see, for example, that a certain Jovan Kulic could never have been a volunteer of the SRS, and therefore you've falsely represented him. You could also have clarified which Chetnik Vojvodas were promoted to that rank because they were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and which were granted that title because they had fought on various fronts within part of the regular armies of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Serb Krajina and then later on joined the SRS and were granted that title because of their merits, yet now you say you felt no need to apply to the SRS to gain access to their archives because some members of the OTP felt uncomfortable there. I assume you would not have introduced yourself as a prosecutor, but as an objective expert who wanted to write an expert report objectively. You are, in advance, narrowing down your sources, and one can see here that you have no idea about the military organisation or the events surrounding military organisation in the course of this war. So that is a fundamental, methodological omission on your part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will only answer to what I understand to be the question. I don't agree that I ignored important sources. I think, for example, that even more than the documents on the SRS war staff, the articles that were published in "Velika Serbia" are essential to understand not only the role of the Radical Party and Mr. Seselj in the dispatching of volunteers, SRS volunteers, but more specifically the ideology that is driving these volunteers while they're participating in the conflict. And, for example, the information on Jovan Kulic, I drew that from 65 ter number 958, which is an article published in number 12 of "Velika Serbia," and I'm just looking for the title. It's called "Diary of a Volunteer in the Kragujevac Chetnik Detachment," by Srecko Radovanovic where he mentions his activities as an SRS volunteer, if I'm not wrong, in Eastern Slavonia as well as Western Slavonia and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, Srecko Radovanovic doesn't say anywhere that Jovan Kulic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party. He even represents him as a captain first class, isn't that right, and that it's a Chetnik detachment of volunteers from Kragujevac. Kragujevac sits in the centre of Serbia and Jovan Kulic comes from the north of Vojvodina somewhere, so he didn't belong to the Kragujevac Volunteer Detachment by virtue of his origin. How come you didn't observe that? Srecko did cooperate with him but Pulic [as interpreted] did not belong to the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. It wasn't the party that sent him there.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that Jovan Kulic does not originate from Kragujevac, he originates from Novi Sad, which is indeed located in Vojvodina. However, the article, and it would maybe be helpful to see it, indeed shows that Kulic and Radovanovic are cooperating, and I think it's even mentioned in the same line, and one could draw from that the conclusion that actually Kulic also part of that Kragujevac Chetnik Detachment. Now, how he became a member, I cannot draw any conclusions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you remind me of a historian who, when writing a study, doesn't feel like digging in archives, so he uses newspaper articles. You are unable to make a proper selection of sources. In your view, a newspaper article has an equal value to an authentic document, isn't that right, and its journalists who write newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the article is published in a party magazine which is, according to the information found in the party magazine, has been found and is edited by Mr. Seselj. I believe that that information is worthwhile to consider in the context of a report that discusses the role of organisations, volunteer groups and others affiliated with that party in the conflict. Now, as to the importance of open source, including newspapers in research, I think that is another discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where does it say, Mr. Theunens, that I participated in editing "Velika Serbia"; where did you find that information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you take the -- you have the magazine and you take the first page, there is the editorial and it lists who are the journalists who participate in the magazine, where it is printed and so on. At least in one of the issues of "Velika Serbia," and I can give you the ERN of that page, 0116-2337, it says that it's established and edited by Mr. Vojislav Seselj. Secondly, Article 78 of the Statute of the SRS, which is 65 ter number 1990, states that "Velika Serbia" is the SRS Party magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you lying, Mr. Theunens? It doesn't say anywhere here that I established and edited the magazine. It just says that I'm the founder and publisher, founder, the person who set it in motion, and the publisher, the owner, that is. Where does it say that I edited "Velika Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that Mr. Seselj and myself are talking about the same thing. Maybe in the translation, certain words have gone wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the founder and publisher is not the editor. "Velika Serbia" always had an editor-in-chief. The first one was Srjan Glamocanin. He was followed by Sinisa Aksentijevic, and now it's Elena Bozic-Taljan [phoen]. Three editors-in-chief took their turns in that position, and my name is nowhere to be found there. Why would I, as a president of the party and deputy, also edit the party newspaper? I can't do everything in the party, can I?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to come back to the origin of the question, the fact that Mr. Seselj claims himself or states himself that he's the founder and the publisher, in my view, when doing my analysis and applying the intelligence cycle, i.e., checking the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information, allowed to conclude for me that articles on the activities of SRS volunteers published in "Velika Serbia" were an important and reliable source in the context of the report I compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I catch you lying and then you want to answer some other question. Well, let's move on to a third one, then. We have already established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. I don't feel that the witness has lied, because what is the problem? We are faced with this "Velika Serbia," the official magazine of the SRS, which results from the implementation of Article 78 of the statute of that party. Mr. Theunens, have you looked up, in order to determine whether articles could be written in this magazine outside of any control of the party or was there a control on the content of the magazine by the party? So, politically speaking, were the journalists independent politically from the party, the party being the publisher of the magazine? This question may be a bit complex. You may say that you are not in a position to answer or else you may answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not in a position to answer, but I can only, I mean, provide this information, and that is that the articles on the role of SRS volunteers are corroborated by other reports I have seen, and, for example, one report by Srecko Radovanovic, actually this article -- this is 65 ter number 958. The text can also be found in a report Radovanovic sent to the SRS war staff. Yes, I was looking for the 65 ter number, but I don't remember that by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you also mentioned the decision on disbanding the Serbian -- the Chetnik movement of 1994, isn't that right, but you omitted to quote the reasons why the Serbian Chetnik movement was being disbanded. Do you remember those reasons?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that I write about -- or that I include the date for the abolishment of the Serbian Chetnik movement, and this is on page 32 of the second part of the report, English page 32, but, no, I haven't included the reasons why. But maybe they can be found in 65 ter number 2042, which I use as the source of this information on the disbanding of the Serbian Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, can that be put on the screen, that document? I wasn't going to deal with it, but now I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, could we have this document displayed, number 2042.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, would you be so kind as to read out the reasons listed for the dissolution of the movement, 1, 2, 3, and we'll see if there are any on the following page.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. First: "Today, all the volunteers fighting for the freedom of the Serbian people are called Serbian Chetniks, regardless of whether they are members of the Serbian Radical Party or not. "2. The nature of the Chetnik movement is deeply patriotic and freedom-loving, but now when it is well established, it should not be placed into a party-related, ideological or political framework. "3. The Chetnik movement today is completely realised because it is universally accepted by the entire Serbian population in all Serbian states as a position, orientation and tradition."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on the next page?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "4. Powerful Serbian armies were formed in the endangered Serbian states and their unity, in terms of leadership and command, should not be disrupted." Then we shall have to go to the next page: "5. The enemies of the Serbian people tried to abuse the formal organisation of the Serbian Chetnik movement as proof of their claim that paramilitary organisations are active in the Serbian states, although Chetnik volunteers acted exclusively under the command of the Serbian Army in the war. "6. The duplicating of the boards of the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik movement in the internal structure of the party of the Serbian radicals caused occasional misunderstandings and struggle over authority. "7. Members of other political parties also joined the Serbian Chetnik movement, which caused collision in their political work."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Theunens, that in Republika Srpska and in the Republika Srpska Krajina, starting from 1991, various Chetnik organisations were formed which had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party and its section entitled the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my report I have included information on Nikodin Cavic, who was, according to the report by Colonel Tolimir, the chief of security and intelligence administration at the VRS Staff, the president of the SRS in Banja Luka, so Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have also included a document from the chief of the SRS war staff to Nikodin Cavic. Articles, for example -- there's an article in "Velika Serbia" on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Judge, sir, that's not an answer to my question. He's just wasting my time. I want the witness to answer my questions, not to talk about other matters and tell stories that have nothing to do with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness should allow -- the witness should be allowed to answer the question, or the accused must put some short questions that the witness can answer in short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've noted that when the question is very lengthy, the answer may be lengthy as well, so perhaps that short questions might lead to short answers, or else you're wasting your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness tried to represent as his answer is a story about the Serbian Radical Party, about Nikodin Cavic who was its founder in Banja Luka, and so on and so forth. My question was: Is the witness aware that beyond the reach of the Serbian Radical Party and its Serbian Chetnik movement, starting in 1991, on the territories of the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, a rather large number of independent organisations sprang up which referred to themselves as Chetnik, or "ramna gorski" [phoen], and they had nothing to do with SRS, and the witness can answer that with a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm aware of that, but the reason I gave the other information is that I included -- I was very careful not to include such information in my report, because indeed there were different groups using the name "Chetnik." However, I wish just to conclude, to draw your attention to a statement -- public statement Mr. Seselj made in June 1991, where he states that the SCP had established a Chetnik command in Romanija, and that is 65 ter number 267 to be found on page 166 of the second part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I remember, Mr. Theunens, that statement of mine from 1991. But as you have heard of it, did you check whether such a Chetnik command was actually established in Romanija at that time, or was I making a statement for propaganda reasons saying that the Chetnik command had been formed? That was the year before the war in Bosnia. I had heard that the Muslims had formed a paramilitary organisation, and the green berets, and to counter them I said that the Chetnik command had been established in Romanija. But did you investigate whether it was actually been done? No, you didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I looked -- Your Honours, I looked into -- I looked at -- I checked for information which would allow to corroborate or deny this statement made by Mr. Seselj, and I have not been able to identify such information, so I cannot draw any conclusion as to whether this Chetnik command in Romanija became active or not, and if it became active, when it became active. But there is, for example, the article -- the interview with Slavko Aleksic, a Chetnik Vojvoda. Slavko Aleksic was the commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment who stated that even though initially he was a member of the SDS, he quite soon joined the SRS and organised his own -- in consultation with the SRS in Belgrade, organised his own chapter of the Serbian Chetnik movement in his area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the problem that any reasonable Judge may have regarding this is that Judges may observe that many crimes have been committed by a number of various individuals who might, and I insist on this, "might," might have been members of political parties, and listening to your answers we discover that there were volunteers on the ground who had different political affiliations. There were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, but there were also other volunteers. There were other volunteers. So there might be some confusion in the mind of people who would not be sufficiently informed about the various aspects of the Chetnik Movement, because in 1991, as we can see, the Chetnik Movement is related to many various things, whereas, as we heard, the leaders of this movement didn't want to control anything else than what they had under their control. And apparently many efforts were made to allege that a number of things that were not done by them were done by Seselj's volunteers. So it is quite important to examine everything that was done in various areas and determine what was a crime and what was not a crime; and if this has been done, then there is no problem alleging that a given political party may be responsible or not. So this is, you see, this is the issue as far as that kind of thing is concerned. What can you tell us about this, as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm conscious of the problem, and what I have attempted to do, while drafting the report, is to always make the distinction. And when, for example, the term "Chetnik" was used, to always verify whether the use of that term referred to any linkage which would be relevant in the context of my report, i.e., linkage to the SRS, members of the SRS or the SRS war staff, or including Mr. Seselj. And when I talk about SRS volunteers in various areas, I have included documents from various sides, if I can express myself that way. There will be military documents, but there will also be documents from the radical party, including "Velika Serbia" articles. In this context, the two orders, the order number 125 and the order number 425, and they are 65 ter number 1841 and 2030, and they have been tendered, these orders, where people -- where senior volunteers are proclaimed Chetnik Vojvoda, are extremely helpful in this context, because for each of the volunteers they include a short CV, including the areas where these volunteers were active, and as well as information on their relation with the SRS or the Serbian Chetnik Movement or the SRS war staff while they are active as volunteers. And this is really -- this has really been the -- yeah, the driving factor while compiling the report, is to always make the distinction between claims like Chetniks or other volunteers and information where a factual link between the volunteers and the SRS can be established. And I hope that this is also visible while reading the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll carry on after the break. It is 10.30. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that some other political parties in Serbia, in taking over the Chetnik traditions, proclaimed Serbian Chetnik Vojvodas?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know that the popular party of Milan Paroski proclaimed some 15 Chetnik Vojvodas, and the Chetnik Vojvoda from World War II joined them. His name was Markovic-Tularski, Milos Markovic-Tularski. I'm not quite sure with regard to his first name, but the surname is certainly correct. That is a Chetnik Vojvoda who, towards the end of the war, joined the partisans, and the communists after the war didn't touch him because of that, but there were a number of public attacks on him, and within the National Populist Party he proclaimed some 15 Chetnik Vojvodas. Do you know that the Serbian Realist Bloc, in accepting the Chetnik traditions, proclaimed Sinisa Vucinic as a Chetnik Vojvoda. Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm familiar with the name Milan Paroski. Now, when I used the term "vojvoda" in my report, I always verified whether these were Vojvodas that had been -- or Chetnik Vojvodas that had been proclaimed by the SRS, and the source I used for that were the two orders discussed earlier, order number 124 and number 425, which have been tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the new piece of information we have here, which was not contained in your report and which so far I knew nothing about, is that the term "Vojvoda" was given by other political parties, other than the SRS. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while preparing my report, I came across the use of the term "Vojvoda" with names I could not link to the Serbian Radical Party, and these may well be Vojvodas who may have been proclaimed by other parties or maybe self-proclaimed Vojvodas who said, "Well, from tomorrow on, I'm a Vojvoda." But I don't think it has any direct relevance for my report, because as I mentioned, in my report, when I use the term "Vojvoda," I have made sure that we're talking about Vojvodas who have been proclaimed by the Serbian Radical Party, and more specifically by an order signed by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you've just inadvertently answered my next question now. You said that you came across, in the documents, the existence of self-proclaimed Chetnik Vojvodas, and that's precisely what my next question was going to be. But you've already answered that question now. But what does that mean, Mr. Theunens? Does that mean that the Chetnik tradition took root and was not localised to just one political party? That's the essential question, as far as I'm concerned, because you can see there was a number of political parties that followed those traditions, even the Serbian -- the Vuk Draskovic Movement to Serbian renewal, although they formed the Serbian Guard paramilitaries, but they followed Chetnik traditions, too, did they not? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: While preparing the report, Your Honours, indeed I came across various information indicating that what was called "Chetnik tradition" was quite popular among the nationalistic political parties and was used as a kind of, yeah, motivation or ideology for their volunteers or their own organisations. Now, as I said earlier, I have been very careful in my report to make sure that when I use the term "Chetnik," it can always be linked through documents to the SRS war staff. I did not concern myself, in my report, with the indiscriminate use of the term "Chetniks" by groups who had nothing to do with the SRS or the SRS war staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it's important to me that you confirm here that there were different Chetnik groups that had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party and that there were quite a lot of other parties who all -- which also revived the Chetnik traditions and were guided by them. Is that a correct observation here on my part? Don't think about it and wonder what Mr. Marcussen is going to say to your answer. Just confirm what I've just said. You can't wriggle out of this. You have to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen has got nothing to do with this, for the time being. Mr. Theunens, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My answer is that I've come across information indicating that groups not affiliated with the SRS also used the terms "Chetnik" and "Chetnik tradition."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you know, Mr. Theunens, that the Serb adversaries in this war, and it was a civil war, in essence, the Muslims, Croats, called or referred to all Serb soldiers "Chetniks." They even referred to the JNA as the "Serbo-Chetnik Army." Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the use of, in general, derogatory terms to characterize or to identify the opposing side by all sides in the conflict, including the use of "Chetniks" by the opposing side, i.e., Croats, Bosniak or Muslims and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can we deduce from that a joint conclusion, which is that when it is said somewhere that certain Chetniks performed -- perpetrated a war crime, for example, that does not automatically mean that those Chetniks mentioned were automatically the members of the Serbian Radical Party; would you agree with that? It doesn't mean that automatically, unless you provide proof and evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. If you say you agree, Mr. Theunens, in the end you're going to agree with all my theses. I can see that coming. Now let's take a look at this list of Chetnik Vojvodas that you've mentioned quite a number of times, and it is Exhibit 1841. Firstly, I notice, Mr. Theunens, in your report, and perhaps it's a question of poor translation, but no difference is made between the word "order" and -- "naredba" and "naredjenje," the two words. Is there a distinction between these two words, meaning "order" in your language?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't understood the words Mr. Seselj wants to use. I mean, I heard "order," and the second word I haven't heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please repeat your question, and if possible spell out the word in your own language, the word which means "order" and the word which means "command."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think I need spell it out. "Naredjenje" can be a concept which is used in our country in a sense of "command," an order, a naredjenje, to attack a stronghold. "Naredjenje," an order to carry out an attack, to withdraw, whereas "naredba," an order, can be a legal attack which can be general and individual. So one legal act, that can be referred to as "naredba" can regulate certain matters. For example, I, as president of the Serbian Radical Party, have the right to issue a "naredba" order that at the headquarters, party headquarters, smoking is to be prohibited in all offices. This is "naredba," it's not a command act. Perhaps the distinction does not exist in the English language. I'm not an expert in English for me to be able to say. But it cannot be "order." It is used -- the word "order" here is used in the sense of command, as far as I know. Now, I hope you're not going to discount that from my time, this explanation I've given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I just on the record want to point out a problem that has come up several times. Here the witness is -- I'm sorry, the accused is testifying as to the meaning of certain words. He cannot do that at this stage, and I just -- if the accused wants to put this sort of thing in evidence, he must bring some evidence at some point in time. But I just wonder about confusion down the line that reference is made by the accused to statements he's made during cross-examination of various witnesses as evidence in this case of any fact. So I say this to alert the accused to this issue so that he can properly prepare his defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Seselj, you have understood what the Prosecution has said. The witness can only answer a question. So you have understood what this is about, Mr. Theunens. Did you establish any distinction between the order and the command? An order, according to Mr. Seselj, has more of a legal meaning, i.e., an instruction which needs to be complied with, whereas seemingly the word "command" would be less of a binding nature, anything that comes under the meaning of that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to SFRY Armed Forces doctrine, there's no distinction between an order and a command, except that a command is of a lower level. Looking at the hierarchy of orders that can be given, we start with instructions. Then we have directives. Then we have orders. Then we have commands. Now, in the context of the proclamation of Chetnik Vojvodas, I have not made a distinction. I would just like to add that the key issues in relation to these proclamations, orders as I translated them, for me is that they show the linkage between certain individuals and the SRS war staff or the SRS as a political party, as well as the areas where these individuals were active with SRS affiliated volunteers and what they were doing there. It also shows that people who were given the title or promoted to Vojvoda held a position of authority among their fellow -- among the other SRS volunteers. That was, for me, the main reason to include -- or the key reason to include these orders on the proclamation of Chetnik Vojvodas, and whether these were orders or commands and whether there's a legal distinction or not was not my first preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, Tomislav Nikolic, who was proclaimed the Chetnik Vojvoda under number 12, where did he have authority over other volunteers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be helpful if we would see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is document 1841. But you're going to take up too much of my time, looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we have to move to the next page to see -- for the expert to be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that the CV that is given for Tomislav Nikolic does not provide information on whether or not he was in charge or he led volunteers. I do wish to draw the Judges' attention that on the third line from the top of the page, it is said that in the beginning -- or this is the second line: "In the beginning he organised and fitted out the volunteer units of the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement, he led and actively participated in the battles in Slavonia where he demonstrated ..." And so on and so on. The use of the word "led," for me indicated that he was in the position of authority and that, yeah, he was leading people or volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't say "leading" here, it says "predvodi." When the word "predvodi" is used, it is a political term meaning being a head. It doesn't say command. He wasn't in command, but he was courageous and brave in fighting, and that's why he was proclaimed a Chetnik Vojvoda. But he wasn't the commander of a volunteer unit.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The accused is testifying again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
