utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've noticed this. Mr. Tomislav Nikolic, who is a person who is seemingly quite well known, particularly a while ago, now he is declared a Vojvoda. And according to your report and according to what other witnesses have said, we are to understand that a Vojvoda is some kind of a military chief. In this case, it looks as if we are told that this gentleman had perhaps taken part in fighting in Slavonia, where he would have demonstrated a great deal of courage, but we are not under the impression that he commanded a unit. Mr. Seselj indicated that in English, "led" means that he headed these men, but this doesn't mean that he is commanding the men. So can one be a Vojvoda without necessarily be heading a military unit, and is that not a ceremonial distinction which does not call for or does not have any consequences on anyone's administrative, political or military career? To add to this, in item 13 I see that this person was commanding a unit. This is what's written here. In item 13, "Ostojic," Ostojic was commanding a unit, but the person before him, Mr. Nikolic, seemingly was not commanding a unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Seselj himself defined or gave his definition of the term -- of what he understood under "Chetnik Vojvoda" in an interview that was published in his book "There are many idiots," or it's a chapter that's called "There Are Many Idiots" in his book "Through Political Galimatias," which is to be found in footnote 170 at part 2 of my report, English page 72, where Mr. Seselj says -- sorry, that's 65 ter number 1848. Mr. Seselj says: "The title of Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda is the highest Chetnik title and it is difficult to find a correlation between it and an army rank. The closest would probably be the rank of major general. A Chetnik Vojvoda commanded units up to the size of a division. Perhaps these explanations for the public are not a bad thing." I do agree that Mr. Seselj says "commanded," i.e., that he probably makes a reference to history, and it could be the Second World War or earlier existence of Chetnik Vojvodas. As it is in the military, not every general major is in command of a unit. However, what I've tried to explain in the report is that people who are proclaimed Vojvoda are put in a position of authority, in particular in relation to the other volunteers, which means that you -- in this kind of de facto situation with volunteer units, detachments which are organised according to military lines but are not always formalised in that way, that one can lead people without commanding them. And I see "lead" more as a moral authority, especially in the context of the ideology that is being applied or that is being followed or adhered to by these volunteers. So I agree that a distinction can be made in the context of Chetnik Vojvoda between leading and commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Theunens, that in World War II as well there were Chetnik Vojvodas who never commanded a single Chetnik unit? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have read about the Second World War and how it developed in the territory known as the SFRY, including the existence of Chetnik Vojvodas. I was not aware -- I'm not aware of any specific examples of Chetnik Vojvodas who were not in command of Chetnik units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You therefore have not heard of Chetnik Vojvoda Dobroslav Jevdevic and that French spy, Yves Tomic, heard of him, the member of the French intelligence, he heard of him, and knew that Dobroslav Jevdevic dealt with political issues and negotiations and so on and so forth. And you'll find that in the transcript. You said you followed the testimony of that French spy, Yves Tomic. Did you say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. Beforehand, I knew that Mr. Marcussen was going to raise an objection. Mr. Seselj, Mr. Tomic, the expert, testified. Admittedly, this expert did work for the Ministry of Defence in France, he told us so, but for you to conclude that this gentleman is a spy, I think it's a far cry from this. Why not? But you need to be able to provide evidence, and I understand why Mr. Marcussen stepped in. He's saying -- yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't assume, Mr. President, that in Western countries it's a shame being a spy. We are inundated with these things where spies are the number one figures, James Bond and onwards. It's shameful to be a spy in Serbia, but in Western countries people boast of the fact that they are spies. But let's leave that aside. It's not essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I in command of any Chetnik unit before Vojvoda Momcilo Djujic proclaimed me a Chetnik Vojvoda? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents I reviewed while preparing the report, I've -- I can conclude that certain volunteer -- SRS or SCP volunteer detachment were deployed upon the orders of Mr. Seselj. And when I draw this conclusion, I draw it from the statements of the people who were in charge of these volunteer detachments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that you must give me at least one hour of my time back which this witness intentionally has wasted. I'm asking him whether he knows that I was in command of a Chetnik unit before Vojvoda Djujic proclaimed me to be a Chetnik Vojvoda, does he have any information to that effect, and his answer was that he has information that I ordered somebody over there to deploy in a certain locality, et cetera. What's all that about? He's just gobbling up my time without answering my questions, and this is a serious problem. That was the same thing with Oberschall and Yves Tomic and it's repeating itself. And is it the Prosecution that is systematically preparing its witnesses in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there's some misunderstanding here. From what I understood, Mr. Seselj is asking you whether you saw any documents that established that he had commanded volunteer units in the way a Vojvoda commands his men, and you answered by saying, "Yes," seemingly, and you said that you had reviewed a number of documents, and you indicated that you did have documents that established that Mr. Seselj did send volunteers on the ground. So that is the way in which you answered this question. So you have not avoided his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I call myself -- self-proclaim myself Chetnik Vojvoda? Did I deserve that by having commanded a Chetnik unit prior to that, before that, before I was given the title?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we now have a very precise question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I apologise for missing that part of the question. No, I didn't come across any information indicating that Mr. Seselj was in command of Chetnik units prior to the 28th of June, 1989, when Momcilo Djujic, who was the chairman of the movement of Serbian Chetniks of Ravna Gora, proclaimed him Chetnik Vojvoda. And, excuse me. The document that explains the motives for Djujic to appoint Seselj -- Mr. Seselj to -- or to proclaim him a Chetnik Vojvoda can be found on page 73 of part 2 of the report, and is 65 ter number 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Theunens, that the title of Chetnik Vojvoda can have some military equivalent from a captain first class to major general in rank, and you quoted me there, but it does not necessarily have a military equivalence, so it needn't be strictly related to any military functions and the performing thereof; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I will repeat myself, that it doesn't have to mean "command," but from looking at the documents included in the report, I draw the conclusion that a Vojvoda is a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Theunens. You've been asked a very specific question, and I'll ask it again on my own behalf. Is it possible to be proclaimed a Vojvoda without having had a military command prior to that? Mr. Seselj is giving you his own example. He was proclaimed a Vojvoda, whereas he had no military command. Therefore, the answer should be "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is "yes." Indeed, the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at the list, 124, on the proclamation, and answer this question first: Why, very often in your report, instead of using the term "proclamation" being proclaimed a Chetnik Vojvoda, you use the term "promotion" instead of "proclamation"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I use these terms interchangeably. Why? Because from looking at the short CV that was included in -- for each individual in the proclamation orders, and at the same time looking at the position held by these individuals, the fact of being proclaimed a Vojvoda also included a promotion, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a Belgian national. You speak French as well. You know that there can't be any confusion between "proclamation" and "promotion." The impact of these two events are not the same. We can review all the Vojvodas here, starting with Aleksic at number 1, and apparently some of them were proclaimed Vojvodas without receiving a promotion. Let's take the case of Nikolic, the most significant case. He was proclaimed a Vojvoda, but what did it bring to him? He did not receive any promotion, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the orders indeed state "I proclaim." Now, I didn't see such an important distinction between proclaiming and promoting. The effect is that from the day they are proclaimed Vojvoda, these people identify themselves or are identified by others as Vojvodas. Now, I don't claim that it included an increase in pay, rank, or military rank or whatever. No, I just state that from the day they are proclaimed Vojvoda, they consider themselves, and also the others, in particular the volunteers that are part of the detachments, as a Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take number 10, Kameni. He was the commander of the Leva Supoderica Volunteer Unit. He was proclaimed a Vojvoda. Did he change anything in his military activities? What did it bring to him? What promotion would he have obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't come across documents indicating any participation of Lancuzanin in the conflict after 1992. So when he's proclaimed a Vojvoda in 1993, it's difficult to draw any conclusion as to whether the proclamation to Chetnik Vojvoda has any military impact for Lancuzanin. However, for others, Slavko Aleksic, I think he's number 1 on the list, there we -- I see from the other documents I have consulted that he's considered a self-proclaimed Vojvoda by the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And I've also included in my report a document where the Command of the VRS Sarajevo Romanija Corps provides a very negative assessment of this whole Chetnik Vojvoda proclamation ceremony and the bad affect it has in his view on overall morale and discipline. And that document, that specific is included in my report. Maybe we can Slavko Aleksic, number one. It's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please display number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksic is the commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment already prior to being proclaimed Vojvoda, but from the documents, VRS documents including the Sarajevo section of part 2 of the report, we can see that he is considered or he is called a Vojvoda, or a self-proclaimed Vojvoda, after being proclaimed a Vojvoda. So it has something implications on the level of authority the person has or his level within the structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, hold on, because I'm unsure about the importance of this issue of whether a Vojvoda is someone who has commanded Chetnik units in battle. Now, I understand you to mean that normally the title of a Vojvoda is awarded to someone who has led Chetnik forces in battle and has done so convincingly, but you also then seem to say that, in your own case, you were appointed a Vojvoda without having ever taken part in active battle and without having commanded a Chetnik unit. In the letter in which you were appointed, and I'm quoting from the letter of 28 June signed by Momcilo Djujic, it does say that: "You have joined the first combat ranks to fight for freedom for the Serbian people and the restoration of the Serbian state." And it goes on to say that you have recognised the -- or you have been recognised for your "heroic struggle and resolute conduct." And yet if you go on on the next page in the expert report, you will see that according to the SRS documentation, the rank of Chetnik was used during the conflict in Croatia and BiH "to honour volunteers who had distinguished themselves during battle." And I'm quoting from page 74 of part 2 of the expert's report. Now, my question to you, Mr. Seselj, is: What is the significance of a Vojvoda having fought in battle? Why is it important for us to understand that sometimes apparently Vojvodas can be appointed even if they have not taken part in active combat?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part of your question, with respect to my proclamation, well, there's "combat" mentioned, "fight" mentioned, it's my dissident struggle, why I went to prison, why my books were banned, and why for years I was persecuted. It wasn't an armed struggle, but it was an important struggle, because as a Serb nationalist I was resolute in fighting the communist regime. Now, on the basis of that, Vojvoda Djujic thought that I merited the title. Now, here, from this proclamation, what you can see is this, that the Chetnik Vojvodas were not proclaimed with this title in order to command units, but they received the title of Chetnik Vojvoda subsequently, once they had proved themselves successful in commanding units. Some of these people were officers holding ranks. Kameni -- Lancuzanin Kameni was a reserve first class captain by rank; Slavko Crnic was a major of the Army of Republika Srpska; Slavko Aleksic was a lieutenant; Nedeljko Vidakovic, lieutenant again. So some of them had army ranks, others didn't. But after so many years, and this dates to 1993, so they were fighting for two years already and were in command of certain units, as a mark of recognition for their heroic struggle and discipline, I give them this title. It didn't mean any promotion, it didn't carry along with it any promotion, nor did anybody have to recognise it. The title itself was an honourable thing to be proclaimed. He could command after that or never command anybody after that. But it's a token of respect, and people refer to that person as "Vojvoda," just like the British title "sir," and then people refer to somebody who has been knighted as "sir." So on the basis of his merits he is given the title of Vojvoda and then people refer to him, when addressing him say "Vojvoda." And he has a certificate saying that he is truly a Chetnik Vojvoda, so it's outside any military hierarchy. And taking my example and the example of Tomislav Nikolic, we can see that we gained this title as politicians, not as commanders. Afterwards, we'll get to what I ordered and what I could order once the war had already broken out, but the title of Chetnik Vojvoda is something that I was given far before any war broke out; in 1989, in fact. So that's the crux of the matter and the essence of it, and I think that needed to be explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, we've just listened to this rather long statement of Mr. Seselj, and from what I understand, that according to him this is an honorary title that is given to someone after the events. It's a title that may be used that the holder of this title, because this person might still be in command of a particular unit, but that is not necessarily the case. Do you agree with this explanation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the party statute of the SRS in Article 85, and this is 65 ter number 1990, actually explained that Vojvoda is a rank, and this is on page 74 of my report, so I don't agree with the definition Mr. Seselj gives. I think that even though he doesn't include a military promotion as to a military rank which is recognised within the SFRY Armed Forces, the attribution or the -- of the title or rank of Vojvoda increases the authority of the particular volunteer among his other SRS volunteers within his volunteer group, and he uses that title during battle. And the other parties that are involved, for example, the VRS, are aware of the title being used and don't necessarily recognise it and call him then a so-called Vojvoda. But it's more than an honourific title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently we are -- the question is now whether this is a title or a rank. Our expert witness tells us that under Article 85 of the party statute, it is a rank.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to be shown here. I can't have all the papers before me, Judge, sir. If he told us what number it is, let's see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have document 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1990, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1990. Article 85 just quoted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's on page 7 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, you can see that we're being misled here. In Article 85, it says the title of Vojvoda can be granted to an individual who cumulatively meets the following conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please read Article 85 in your own language, because in English we see the word "rank." Please read it out in your own language, and the interpreters will translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original word is "zvanje." Let the interpreters confirm, it's a "zvanje," not "rank"...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Zvanje," literally means "location," the interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... can be granted to a person who achieves the following -- who fulfills all the following conditions: As distinguished fighter in all fields of the Serbian peoples struggle for Serbian national rights. So that means in all domains, the political domain, the cultural domain, it doesn't have to be an armed struggle, for the defence of Serbian national rights. And then a distinguished fighter for the defence of Serbdom and the honour, dignity, culture, and traditions of the Serbian people, that he is respected in his living and working environment, that he's a participant in combat, a model soldier and officer, at the time when the Serbs are conducting their defensive war, in times of war, whenever war is waged. But you can also become a Vojvoda when there is no war. This article is so clear that it solves all the problems being created by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to you a while ago was: Why is it important for the Chamber to understand this distinction? What is the significance in relation to your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expert keeps insisting that acquiring the title of Vojvoda brought new power to a person. My case is that acquiring the title of Vojvoda brought no particular power, only honour. That's my case, and that's why it's important, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, when Mr. Seselj read out Article 85, the interpreter from the French booth used the word "titre," "title" and not the word " grade" or "rank." Therefore, according to Article 85, "title," then, not a rank is being awarded; and if it's a title, it does not imply that someone will receive a promotion, be in command of anything, or it doesn't mean the same thing. What do you think, because you speak French as well as English, you're perfectly aware of the difference between "rank" and "title"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, there is a distinction. I mean, it's a different word. In English, it was translated as "vocation." But when I come back to the report, I -- and I will just summarise that, I do not claim that when somebody becomes -- is proclaimed Vojvoda that suddenly he's put in command of a unit. As we can see from the proclamation order, some of these people were already in command. The least we can say is that the proclamation to Vojvoda confirms their position of command, if they were in command before, and if not, the least one can say -- or in addition one can also say that actually it confirms their authority over the volunteers. And that was, for me, the most important aspect in the whole debate over Vojvodas and the authority and the powers they had. Looking at the volunteer groups or detachments, the SRS volunteer detachments, how they were organised, how they operated, I believe that it's of key importance to know that certain people who were in command of these detachments were actually confirmed by Mr. Seselj or their authority was being confirmed through the proclamation to Chetnik Vojvoda, and that this proclamation to Chetnik Vojvoda also had an effect on the respect and the authority these Chetnik Vojvoda enjoyed from their volunteers in their detachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I can just suggest that I think we -- there might be a discrepancy in the English and the French translation of the word "zvanje," which is used in the English transcript at page 65, line 14, and I don't blame the interpreters, who have to do this on the fly. I was going to suggest that maybe the Chamber direct the CLSS to file a short note which explains these terms so we have that on the record and allow the interpreters time to come up with a right definition in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll ask the CLSS to provide a translation of this word. But let me come back to your previous answer, Mr. Theunens. You stated that the rank or title of Vojvoda gives authority to the holder of this title. In normal times, I would agree with you, but when you look at a document, when you find a document that proclaims someone to the rank or title of Vojvoda a few months or a few years after the events, then it does not add up. Let's take the case of Kameni. Unfortunately, I don't have the document in front of me. That's why I do not like working with the e-court system. It's really a handicap for me, as a judge, because if I had the document in front of me, I would have been able to check immediately on what date this order was issued by Mr. Seselj for the proclamation of these Vojvodas. When he was proclaimed a Vojvoda, the Vukovar events had already taken place, so it was not going to give him any additional authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honours in relation to Lancuzanin. The order dates from the 13th of May, 1993. But when I say "authority," it is authority within this organisation of the Serb Radical Party including the volunteer detachments this Radical Party has in the field. It is true that we have no information on the participation of Milan Lancuzanin in the conflict after 1992. Now we can only speculate on what the title of Vojvoda meant in practice for Lancuzanin. But the reason why I spoke about authority among the volunteers who were part of the detachment the Vojvodas were in charge of, I was referring to people like, for example, Aleksic who were already in command of a detachment prior to the proclamation to Vojvoda as well as afterwards. I also put in my report that the people in charge -- or it were the Chetnik Vojvodas who were in charge of SRS volunteer detachments. Even if they were proclaimed SRS detachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you, because we are spending a lot of time on this. If you take the case of Aleksic, I would agree with you if the proclamation indeed gave him additional authority as a commander, but to establish that, we would have need to check -- need to check that as soon as he was proclaimed Vojvoda, the unit he belonged to or the services he belonged to gave him additional tasks, a promotion, and I don't have this information, I don't have it. What I have is your statement, and what you tell us is not supported by any evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I use the word "authority" in the context of volunteer detachments, I use it in a less formal way than you use it. It has to do with, yeah, authority in the sense of authority as a human being among these volunteers. We see the volunteers were part of Aleksic's detachment, see that their commander is being confirmed by the president of the Radical Party, who is the basis for their ideology and the reason why they participate in the conflict, see that their commander is being confirmed not only in his position as commander, but he's actually given an additional call it title or rank by the president of the party, and that's what I mean by the authority of the Chetnik Vojvoda among his volunteers. It's an informal thing with, of course, effects in practice on the functioning of that individual as a commander of a volunteer detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, are you able to answer the following brief questions with just a "yes" or "no," please? Did Slavko Aleksic, a volunteer whom the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia sent from Serbia to fight at the Sarajevo front; yes or no? Was Slavko Aleksic a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the translation, but Slavko Aleksic was born in Sarajevo and he was not sent to Sarajevo by the SRS, but he joined -- I think the article in "Velika Serbia" stated that he was first a member of the SDS. He was unhappy with the SDS, and he then sought contact with the SRS in Belgrade and established a local department of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I must ask you once again to give me short answers. Do you have information showing that the Serbian Radical Party, in the unit commanded by Slavko Aleksic throughout the war, and that was a company of a certain brigade of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that the Serbian Radical Party sent a single volunteer to that unit ever?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- I'm -- I don't have such information. However, I believe that it would be helpful to show or to have a look at 65 ter number -- one second. I'm just looking for the 65 ter number in my report. Yeah, I will come back with the 65 ter number later. But, anyway, there's an article, a "Velika Serbia" article on Slavko Aleksic and it describes also the circumstances how he became in charge of his volunteers, and actually -- yeah, I will find it -- I will find it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why talk for so long, Mr. Theunens, when you have not a shred of evidence that a single volunteer was sent to that unit by the Serbian Radical Party? As for Mirko Blagojevic, a volunteer whom the Serbian Radical Party sent from Serbia to Bijeljina to fight, was that so; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the statements Mirko Blagojevic made, and I believe that you, yourself, Mr. Seselj, made statements on the involvement of -- on the role played by Blagojevic in Bijeljina, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's correct that we sent him to Bijeljina from Serbia to fight or that we did not send him? Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was -- I mean, what is correct is there was a link between Blagojevic and the Serb Radical Party, and I want to -- I think it's better if we use documents to illustrate what we are trying to say. That is 65 ter number 1032, where Mr. Seselj -- this is a press conference on the 9th of April, 1992, where Mr. Seselj identifies Mirko Blagojevic as the chairman of the Serbian Radical Party, regional board for Northeastern Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is all being broadcast on the internet. The public is following the way you are undermining my cross-examination. I'm asking you a very concrete question. Did we send him to fight from Serbia or was he from Bijeljina, born in Bijeljina, where the war found him? That's the essence of my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on my recollection, Blagojevic was from the area, so he was not sent from Serbia. But what I'm trying to -- I'm trying to explain the links between the role or the participation of Blagojevic in the conflict in Bijeljina and the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, don't explain things I'm not asking you about. My questions are quite concrete. I had links with Vladimir Seks, the speaker of the Croatian Parliament, because he was an anti-communist dissident before the war, so he visited Belgrade and socialised with me, but we were not on the same side in this war, so what does that mean? According to your documents, did the Serbian Radical Party ever send a single volunteer from Serbia under the command of Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two questions, I think, because I think the first question deals with the linkage between Blagojevic and the Radical Party, and the second question deals with whether or not the Radical Party sent volunteers to Bijeljina. For the second part -- --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, put a stop to this. I don't have the patience to listen to this. I didn't put two questions now, but only one: Did the Serbian Radical Party ever send a single volunteer under the command of Mirko Blagojevic? That was my question. You are tolerating this waste of time. I ask that he answer my questions with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did the Serbian Radical Party send Blagojevic to Bijeljina as a volunteer of the party, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do we mean by "send" that he was sent from Belgrade, or do we mean by "send" that he participated in the conflict in Bijeljina as a person in charge or in command of Serbian volunteers, SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This again is a language problem. "Sent," to send. According to your report, we get the feeling that certain people were leaving Serbia to get to the ground outside of Serbia, so there's a move, but in the recent time we have also heard evidence that allows us to believe that certain local people like Kameni, for example, that certain locals were joining the Serbian Radical Party, so these people joined the party, they are not sent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the question better now, Your Honours. Blagojevic was from the area, and Mr. Seselj himself stated that, "It were not our units from over here, i.e., from Belgrade, but our local members from over there did it," headed by Mirko Blagojevic. Mirko Blagojevic is a Vojvoda. And this is an expert which is mentioned on English page 179 of part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Mirko Blagojevic, after the 13th of May, 1993, when he was proclaimed the Chetnik Vojvoda, ever participate in a single battle after that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't come across any documents indicating participation of Blagojevic in battles after his proclamation to Chetnik Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the next on the list, Branislav Vakic was a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party who was sent to the front from Serbia. After he was proclaimed the Chetnik Vojvoda, however, do you have a shred of evidence that he participated in the war again after his proclamation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be helpful if I could see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The document is in front of you. Here it is on the screen. Let them turn the next page in English. You can see it in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't come across any documents indicating that Vakic -- or showing Vakic's participation in the conflict after his proclamation to Chetnik Vojvoda on 13th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please answer "yes" or "no" so we can move faster. With regard to Nedeljko Vidakovic, was he a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party who we sent from Serbia to Herzegovina to fight in the war? He's the fourth on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute before the witness answers. Mr. Seselj, if you go one by one to each of the people on the list, you will waste a lot of time. I remind you that you are left with less than two hours. So if you have important topics to address, you had better do that. If you list all these people, it will take quite a lot of time. It's for you to decide, of course, but it's your free choice, but I'm calling your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is very important to me because it provides the answer to innumerable questions. But I ask that you and your colleague, Mr. Harhoff, issue a decision making up for the time that has been wasted by the -- by the attitude of the witness. We have wasted a lot of time because of his extensive replies and avoidance of responding to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... give additional time, depending on the useless speech, as you call it, of a witness. It is for the person who is asking the questions to take into consideration the personality facing him and doing what has to be done in order to control the answers of the witness. So when you put very lengthy questions, and I already told you this, it calls for lengthy answers. If you want answers by "yes" or "no," put short questions to the witness so as to enable him to answer by "yes" or "no." But you cannot take advantage of a lot of time spent by the witness in answering, you cannot take advantage of this to ask for additional time, because in that case the Prosecution would do the same. It's for you to think about this beforehand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I keep thinking, Judge, and I think at the speed of light, but then I have to wait for a long time until I get a reply, and then the reply is never direct. But if you want to tolerate this, I have no choice but to continue. I don't have much choice. I think it's very important to go through all these Chetnik Vojvodas in order to show that about half of them were volunteers from Serbia who went to fight at the front and that half were local people who, due to their merits in the war after they joined the Serbian Radical Party, were honoured with this high title. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you received three binders of documents yesterday. I asked you to go through them. I hope you have, and I hope that you can answer a few questions based on these binders. The Trial Chamber also has them, and I think there's no need to go through the documents one by one, because all the documents make up a whole. Have you studied these documents, first of all, the ones you got yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I reviewed the documents and I noted that especially in the third binder, there is a lot of translations lacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it clear to you, from the translations you did get and the documents you did get, that all these documents refer exclusively to the participation in the war of three persons: Slavko Aleksic, Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne and Vasilje Vidovic? Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From these documents, can we indubitably see that all three men were within the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: A number of these documents are not dated, so it is actually difficult to make any conclusions in that regard. And a whole lot of -- the majority of the documents are actually outside the indictment period. They are from 1994 and 1995 and later dates. There are also documents from 1992 and so on, but I just wish to point this out so there's no confusion later on about what the record actually is, because we're not apparently going through these documents, but we're talking about 183 documents in bulk, from the way the questions are being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are very aware of the proceedings in this Tribunal. I'm asking you whether Slavko Aleksic has had an indictment against him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Mr. President. I can answer, if you're interested, Mr. President. I can answer straightaway. None of those three were ever indicted by this Tribunal. These three individuals, as Chetnik Vojvodas, gave me all their documents, or rather they provided my assistants with them, and gave me the right to use them in these proceedings. The Prosecution ascribed certain crimes to them. I claim that they are falsely being ascribed these crimes, and I have brought documents which show that they were never -- the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in the area at all, but they were fighters and commanders of the Army of Republika Srpska, and all the documents testify to that. Just one of them came to the Sarajevo battle front, Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne, as a volunteer, and as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Fighting, he took part in the fighting for Grbavica. Once Grbavica was liberated, the volunteers went back to Serbia and he stayed on in Sarajevo, because that's where he was born. And then he went to Ilidza, formed some combat group over there, fought over there. He had problems with his relationships and with his senior officers, superior officers, but at that time he was no longer a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party. And I brought along with me these three binders with documents to eliminate, with one gesture, all the counts in the indictment for Sarajevo. At the relevant time in the indictment, none of these people were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. What they were were officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's what these documents show, and that's what I wanted to ask this witness. If I were to take it document by document, we would go on until the autumn, counting with the speed of which I am receiving answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now under the background. Can you now put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of these documents and military booklets that are attached there, can we see that all three men were soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska throughout the time of the war, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 119, which is in binder number 2 -- I'm just taking an example, but tab 119 in binder number 2 states -- this is the document for Branislav Gavrilovic states, and I will read it out that, okay, permission is given and so on: "For the purpose of Serbian volunteer units which are part of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior for Serbian municipality of Ilidza, the overall command of the SAO Romanija volunteer units, Branislav Gavrilovic, will receive and train Serbian volunteers." So this is one example showing that a group of Gavrilovic, at least at the time of the document, 1992, is not part of the VRS but is part of the forces controlled by the Ministry of Interior. Now, in my report, when looking at the Sarajevo section, I do not conclude that these four SRS/SCP volunteer detachments that were operating in Sarajevo were outside the authority of the VRS. I only conclude that there were quite regularly problems with these units or with these detachments. And, for example, in the binder there are a lot of documents on Vaske. These documents correspond with the documents I include in my report, that Vaske was commander of, sometimes it was called a battle group, Vaske's battle group or Vaske's platoon, whereby this platoon had a military post number and was a unit which belonged to the Ilijas Light Infantry Brigade of the VRS. Notwithstanding that fact, there were problems with Vaske, and these problems are discussed in the report. And, for example, one of these problems has to do with the relationship between Vaske's unit and UNPROFOR, where we see that there is an order coming from Mladic, so the chief of the main --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We'll come to this. Mr. Seselj, put your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, from these documents can we see that Slavko Aleksic and Vaske Vidovic were officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne, during that period of time, that he belonged to the police of Republika Srpska? Do you confirm that, then, because you've already said some of it? At the time, did they have anything at all to do with the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade in matters of manpower for their units, replenishment of manpower with volunteers, let aside the fact that they were members of the Serbian Radical Party and in their living environments acted in that fashion? But in their units, were volunteers sent from Belgrade? Answer me that. Do you have a single piece of evidence to show that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not come across documents that indicated that the Serbian Radical Party sent volunteers from Belgrade, but the documents I have included confirm that there were other links between these volunteer detachments and the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which other links?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these volunteer detachments are, first of all, in VRS documents and even some MUP documents. They are always identified as radicals or they have particular names like the Brnotovsi [phoen], or the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment, or similar names which show that actually the political affiliation of these groups has a particular importance in relation to their activities. If they had no links whatsoever with the Serbian Radical Party, they would just have been considered volunteers or of unit X, Y or Z of the VRS. The fact, for example, that Vaske's unit is identify by "Vaske" in the documents is quite unusual. When studying JNA and VRS documents, I haven't seen any other references to units being identified by the name of their commander. The use of the term "detachment" is unusual, because normally you would have a military-sized unit, a platoon, a company, a battalion and so on. We spoke earlier about articles in "Velika Serbia." There is very, I think in this context, an interesting article in the activities and the situation of Slavko Aleksic and how he established his group. There is also an article in "Velika Serbia" on -- if I'm not wrong, on Branislav Gavrilovic and how his unit, in August 1993, is disbanded on the orders of the VRS Main Staff, and then he joins the unit of Vaske. And these units have names which are quite uncommon in the military context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia, did it send Vasilje Vidovic to Ilijas to the war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be helpful if we could see the earlier promotion order to Vojvoda for Vidovic, which is 65 ter number 2030. It's the order number 425, or the proclamation order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If Your Honours have the binders, the Prosecution binders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- you will find this document in binder 1, two-thirds down in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So under "Vidovic" we see that he's a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The document does not indicate on whose initiative or on whose instruction he returned to Sarajevo after being involved in the conflict in the Knin-Benkovac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why would he return home at somebody's initiative? Isn't it natural that once the war ended in Krajina, for him to return home? Isn't that natural?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if he had been a member of the armed forces, then he would have followed the orders his superiors in the armed forces would have given to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know that after the Vance Plan, the JNA withdrew from Serbian Krajina and that all the volunteers withdrew with it, and then the volunteers went home, they went to their homes; isn't that right, Mr. Theunens? A volunteer won't continue in an army unit, doing his military service, when he did that long ago and completed it long ago?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from documents discussing actually -- or there is at least one document, a report by a security organ, which mentions a Vasilije Vidovic born in Ilijas in connection with the crimes in Skabrnja. I cannot claim that it's the same individual. But, in any event, this Vasilije Vidovic was in Skabrnja as a volunteer, so -- and as we have discussed extensively during the previous days, volunteers did not -- were not always formally part of the armed forces, so their redeployments do not have to be part of a formal redeployment of the armed forces consisting of JNA and TO. And I do not agree with the conclusion that after the Vance Plan, the JNA withdrew from Serbian Krajina, because we know from the documents it was a formal withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, this proclamation order whereby Vidovic becomes a Vojvoda, we know that after 1992 he is on the battleground at Ilijas after he became a Vojvoda. When the order 425 is given, he's still there, and he shows exceptional courage and dedication in the battle, in the battles. But in this document, we find no indication that he's a member of the VRS. He's not a member of the VRS. And what the accused states is that the person mentioned in the documents, in the three binders, are people who are members of the VRS but who do not relate to the -- who are not under the authority of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to finish my question. So these qualities, these virtues that made him a Vojvoda, whether it's a title or a rank, are related to his activities since 1991, since he fought in Knin. He participated in battles in Knin, so this is a reward for Vidovic's military past. This results in his being awarded the title or rank of Vojvoda, and there is no explicit indication that nowadays he's a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not worthy of note, in the context of this report, that the proclamation order does not make any reference to Vidovic's possible role within the JNA or the VRS. However, his connection with the VRS can be established from other documents. As I mentioned earlier, his unit is sometimes known as "Vaske's platoon" or "Vaske's battle group" or "the sabotage platoon." It has a military post number within the VRS Ilijas Light Infantry Brigade, and the details on that can be found on page 231 to 234 in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Before the break that will be taken at 20 past, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have one more question, and then I would like to tender some documents. Now, the next one is 425, Radovan Radovic who was proclaimed a Chetnik Vojvoda in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Radovan Radovic, was it the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia which sent him to Bileca to take part in the war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not been able to identify information that would allow to draw such conclusion, so I can't say whether it was Radical Party or not. I haven't seen any documents indicating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that Radovan Radovic was already a celebrated commander in Herzegovina, at the head of a unit of the army of Republika Srpska, with the rank of officer, and that in 1994 he became a member of the Serbian Radical Party, and after having become a member in 1994, he was proclaimed the Chetnik Vojvoda for his war merits?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, Your Honours. Now, it would be very helpful for me if I could see a document, for example, that links Radovan Radovic to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why would I show you those documents? You're a Prosecution expert. You can look for the documents. You're avoiding documents, in fact. Now, Judges, gentlemen, I would like to tender the exhibit before the first break. 2042 was the number, and it is the decision on disbanding the Serbian Chetnik movement as a section of the Serbian Radical Party. And I'd also like to tender a document under one number, a single number, or rather the three binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to work one document at a time. So, Mr. Registrar, document 2042 -- Mr. Marcussen, you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The three binders contain a whole lot of documents which haven't even been translated yet. Maybe at least if the three binders go in, they should be marked for identification. I think it should also be made clear that the purpose for which these documents are being admitted is only to understand the answers and questions about this and not necessarily -- the documents are not being admitted for the truth of their contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2042 has been translated into English, so he can receive a number. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 2042 will be Exhibit number D16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think a priori no document is to be believed, and when you admitted documents which were proposed by the Prosecutor, you did not say whether you accepted them as truthful or not, as the Trial Chamber. You will come to assess that at the end, so you will be able to assess whether these documents are truthful or not. But such a large number of documents, 186, in fact, prove just one assertion made by the Defence, and that is that Slavko Aleksic, Vasilije Vidovic and Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne, for that part of their participation in the war which is mentioned in the indictment, were not volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party sent from Serbia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just that one thesis by the Defence is confirmed and borne out by those documents, although the contents are diverse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the core of the issue here. The documents do not show that. The documents show that there was a relationship between the JNA and the VRS and these particular three individuals. That is common ground. There is no -- this is in the expert's report. It is part of the Prosecution's evidence that that is indeed the case. There's no dispute on this matter, there's actually no reason to put in evidence on this issue at all. There is no evidence in this about whether or not the -- these people were sent by the SRS, and that's a concern I have about the relevance that the accused wants to say these documents have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had not yet reached the stage of looking at these documents one by one, so the D16 has been admitted. What other documents would you like to tender, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As one document, I propose the three binders to be taken as one document. Those binders contain a total of 186 documents which relate to the most diverse matters of daily military life, but which are a cumulative testimony of the fact that these three men were officers in the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska, and one of them within the frameworks of the police of Republika Srpska, and I'm not challenging what Mr. Theunens said, that Branislav Gavrilovic belonged to the police at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the documents which are in those three binders, you have reviewed them, all of them, haven't you? These documents have a link with three individuals, you confirm this, with the names of three individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a large extent, Your Honours, I believe there is -- there are a number of documents which are unsigned, undated, unstamped, they are handwritten. Okay, they mention the name, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right, but the Prosecution also tendered documents without dates, signatures, and which are handwritten. This is not a sufficient reason to dismiss a document. But my question is whether or not these documents determine the fact that these three individuals were members of the VRS. This is the question. This is the goal of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we look at tab 145, binder number 2, Your Honours, okay, we discussed Branislav Gavrilovic. Now, it mentions the 1st Volunteers Regiment, Savo Derikonja. I know from looking at other documents, and they are discussed in my report, that Savo Derikonja is actually an SRS volunteer detachment. Now, I have not been able to establish whether or not the SRS kept on sending volunteers to the detachment after 1992, but the document, as such, looked at it in isolation, or just in the context of the binder, may lead to misleading conclusions. There are, for example, a number of commendations for Vaske, for Aleksic, included in the binders. These documents may well be authentic. However, all I wish to mention is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right, but the tab 145 is a document which comes from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. Its date is the 14th of December, 1993, and it certifies that Gavrilovic, the commander of the 1st Volunteers Regiment, Savo Derikonja has donated the following weapons and ammunitions to the Ilidza Public Security Station, and then we have the list of weapons and ammunition. So this document establishes that Gavrilovic has given weapons to a police station. As for the conclusions, we'll see later on. But among these documents, are there documents which, according to you, are perhaps not authentic? Are there forged documents? You are the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say that yesterday afternoon, time went fast, and after all 180 documents, I checked the documents. I also checked -- compared the documents with what is in my report. And as has been pointed out, overall there are no big problems. I have not been able to determine that there were fake documents in the binder -- in the binders, sorry, the three of them. I just want to caution that as with any document, it could be misleading to just look at the document in isolation. As you point out in relation to 145, okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is the role of the Judges. Do not interfere with the work of the Judges. The Judges are highly-experienced professionals who are quite able to read a document and relate a document to the other documents admitted in this case. So regarding the documents we are discussing now, are they relevant, are they authentic, reliable, not forged? But we are not discussing their weight, because their weight will be examined at the end of the trial. The value of those documents, according to Mr. Seselj, as evidence comes from the fact that, according to him, it shows that these people were members of the VRS and had not been sent by the Serbian Radical Party. So, Mr. Marcussen, you maintain your objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, before you answer the question, I have another question that I would like to hear your answer to, and that is: Does the Prosecution contest the allegation made by the Defence, that these three gentlemen were indeed members of the VRS? Is that a contested issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I apologise if that wasn't clear. This is quite clear when you look at part 2 of the expert's report. It's being shown that the volunteers on the ground were being affiliated with various structures on the ground, the JNA, the VRS, the MUP, and they were -- they were subordinated to these structures on the ground. The documents here are being forward as evidence of that. That is not contested. The documents are also being put forward for the proposition that you can infer from those, at best, that the volunteers had no relationship with the SRS. There's no indication in any of the documents, as far as I can see, that the documents can speak to those issues. There's no -- there's no evidence about that issue at all in those documents. So the documents are irrelevant to that issue. So to sum up, the documents are relevant to an undisputed issue and they are irrelevant to the second issue they are being put forward to as proof of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's discuss this after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute, please. There might be a misunderstanding, because the Serbian Radical Party is being mentioned here. I'm not contesting the link between these people and the Serbian Radical Party. These three men formed the Serbian Radical Party in Sarajevo. They established it there in 1992. However, they were not sent from Belgrade to go to war there; but as the locals of Sarajevo, they joined the Serbian Radical Party who moved from the Serbian Democratic to the Serbian Radical Party, Slavko Radovic. The other ones were volunteers in other places. Branislav Gavrilovic was in Slovenia and we find him in Trpinja, and I signed for him saying that he was the commander of volunteers over there. The Prosecutor presented that evidence. Vaske Vidovic was in Serbian Krajina as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party. That's not contested, either. But none of those three arrived from Belgrade to Sarajevo to lead volunteer units as a member of the Serbian Radical Party and their volunteers from Belgrade, and that's what these documents show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate over the break. But to sum up, there are two pieces of information that are not unchallenged. Both parties agree on this: A, these three people are members of the SRS and, B, they belong to the VRS. So much for the two points on which both parties agree. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. The Trial Chamber will hand down an oral decision on the request for admission of documents, which are contained in three binders. The Trial Chamber were seized by the accused Seselj of a request to tender a number of documents into evidence. These are contained in three folders. According to the accused, these documents will testify to the fact that three people are purportedly members of the VRS, and it is for this reason that he has asked for these to be tendered into evidence. The Prosecution has submitted that it was opposed to this admission. The Prosecution, however, does not challenge the fact that these three individuals in question were members of the VRS. The Prosecution indicates, furthermore, that these three people were also members of the Serbian Radical Party. The accused responded by he did not challenge the fact that these three individuals were those people who founded the SRS in Sarajevo. Under these conditions, the Trial Chamber holds that the purpose sought by the accused, i.e., to establish that these three people were members of the VRS, is not challenged by the Prosecution, and therefore there is no reason to admit these documents, other than laying an even heavier burden as regards the number of documents tendered. There will be quite obviously in this trial a great deal of documents to be presented. On these grounds, the Trial Chamber dismisses this admission. Mr. Seselj, you wanted these documents to be admitted to establish that these individuals were members of the VRS. As this is not challenged, there is no reason to admit these documents insofar as in the judgement, if the question arises, the Trial Chamber can then simply refer to the transcript, and on the transcript we read that the Prosecution did not challenge the fact that these three people were members of the VRS. Now, as far as the fact that these people are members of the SRS, this hasn't been challenged, either. So much for our decision now. If you feel that some documents could perhaps be challenged as regards certain items, you can then, of course, ask for these documents to be admitted. You can put questions to the witness on these issues to the witness, and you can even show these documents to other witnesses if you feel that these documents are of some importance. Now, if we look at the countdown, you've had three hours and 20 minutes, Mr. Seselj, and you have exactly one hour and 38 minutes left. I shall now give you the floor back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the fact that you have given me the floor, I hope it doesn't enter into my time, what I'm going to say in comment of your decision. It will not be taken from my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this will not be included.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, nothing is clear to me now. What is the basis of my responsibility for any events in Sarajevo mentioned in the indictment? The Prosecution accepts that these three men were members of the Army of Republika Srpska or the police of Republika Srpska. The expert did not say, expressly in his report, that the three of them were sent as volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party to Sarajevo from Belgrade and that the Serbian Radical Party sent its volunteers to their units. They are members of the Serbian Radical Party. Is that the basis of my responsibility? Am I to be held responsible for every crime committed anywhere by any member of the Serbian Radical Party? Is that the basis of my responsibility? I understand nothing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The implication of the Chamber's decision is that the Chamber accepts that the three gentlemen were not sent from Belgrade, but operated out of Sarajevo, where they were members of the local SRS party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I think that that part of the indictment referring to Sarajevo must be dismissed, because if I'm to be held responsible, I can only be held responsible for those men I sent to the front from somewhere in Serbia, and, sent by me, they committed crimes there. So indirectly I'm responsible for that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer your question. You can be held liable for people whom you've sent. If you did not send these people, you are not responsible. But do not overlook the fact that you are held responsible under the indictment for the JCE or under the JCE, and if these individuals, even if they are not directly under your control as regards form 3 of the JCE, you could be held responsibility for all their acts, i.e., the crimes they committed. So this is the answer I can provide you with right now. This is what Mr. Marcussen wishes to say, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm concerned if there's any confusion about the allegations being levied about -- against the accused, as he's representing himself. Maybe I should just, in very short terms, make clear that the Prosecution's joint criminal enterprise, JCE, allegation is that as of about the spring of 1991, there was a common plan in place which included a number of senior Serb leaders, including the accused. That plan included the creation of what the accused has referred to as a greater Serbia. There was a criminal component to this plan, which was to create a mono-ethnic Serbian state, so part of the plan was to expel and forcibly transfer non-Serbs out of areas of Croatia and Bosnia. The accused contributed to this campaign in a number of ways. He made speeches which created the conditions for -- of an atmosphere which allowed for these crimes to be committed. He contributed men to the campaign that was carried out. They are the two main components of the allegations. Now, these men that were put into the conflict areas by the accused operated in conjunction with other Serb forces, so the basis for this -- for the indictment is crimes committed by a big group of people, and the accused contributed to this campaign. Some of the specific crimes charged were committed by the men under, in our view, the accused's control. Other crimes might not have been committed directly by any of Mr. Seselj's men, but it is our case that he is responsible also for those other crimes because they were part of the same criminal plan that Mr. Seselj adhered to. And, therefore, in the context of the specific crime sites, such as Sarajevo, there will be issues about who committed the crimes, but it is important to make clear to the accused that he is charged with the responsibility for all the crimes that were committed pursuant to this scheme of creating a greater Serbia. Now, the accused is smirking, and I take from that that he is fully aware of what the allegations against him actually are, but I hope that this boils down what the nutshell of the JCE case is for the accused, and also clarify the issue of who the perpetrator -- the relevance of the issue of the perpetrators. And I repeat this. Our case is that the crimes charged in the indictment were committed by members of the SRS/SCP or by other members of other forces operating in the relevant areas, and that responsibility under the JCE theory flows to the accused because of his membership of a joint criminal enterprise among a group of leaders in Serbia. These crimes -- the accused is linked to these crimes either directly through his men or through men belonging to other structures that link up to the leadership level. That's one of the -- that's the first type of JCE that's alleged in the indictment. The second one is that there was a joint criminal enterprise between the accused and his men on the ground. So there are two -- these two alternative JCE theories set out in the indictment. And then, of course, in addition to that, we have planning, ordering and instigating and aiding and abetting charge in the indictment. Now, if there is a need, and that is for the Judges to maybe consider, but we would be happy to provide a short written submission which sets this out more clearly if there's any issue about whether the pre-trial brief that has already been filed and the opening statement is clear on this point, because obviously these are key issues that have to be absolutely clear. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Marcussen has just summed up what you are being charged with. He has provided his point of view. He has mentioned, more specifically, the case of Sarajevo, that crimes may have been committed by people who were not members of the Serbian Radical Party, but given the joint criminal enterprise, you will be held responsible for these. This is what the Prosecution has stipulated, so that you understand the problem fully. So I shall give you the floor back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand this very well, Judges, but then another problem arises. According to their theory of joint criminal enterprise, I was in the narrowest circle of conspirators, because they base their JCE on what used to be conspiracy theory in law. A JCE is a new construct. So I am in the innermost circle of conspirators, with Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, Ratko Mladic, Milan Martic, Veljko Kadijevic, Blagoje Adzic, and others. As I am in the innermost circle of conspirators, within this alleged JCE, why this selection? I am then responsible for all the crimes committed on the Serbian side in these wars, so why are any crimes then deduced? I have aspirations to be responsible for all these crimes. When the indictment was being extended under the presidency of Judge Agius, I asked that all the Serbian crimes in this war be ascribed to me. I protest now because the number of my crimes has been reduced. I demand that I be indicted for all the crimes committed on the Serbian side, because only then can the case of the Prosecution concerning a JCE be upheld. I'm being discriminated against here. I am being subject to prejudice. Why should I not be in the innermost circle of conspirators? I always thought I was more important than Slobodan Milosevic, Veljko Kadijevic, Blagoje Adzic, Radovan Karadzic, Ratko Mladic, and Milan Martic. I always considered myself to be more important than them, so I consider this an insult. The number of crimes has been reduced in my case, and I demand that I be accused of all crimes committed by all Serbs in these wars because I'm in the innermost circle of conspirators in the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as forms of responsibility are concerned, crimes committed in certain municipalities, it is they who decide, so if you want them to add more crimes on the list, in terms of your responsibility, well, the Prosecution can amend its indictment with the authorisation of the Trial Chamber whenever it so wishes. Let me add, with the Chamber's permission. So for the time being, the scope of the indictment is very precise, particularly as regards Sarajevo and the surrounding area. As Mr. Marcussen indicated, he has said that to what extent you would be held liable, and I am purposefully using the conditional tense. You may resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I was surprised by the fact that you paid so little attention to the existence of the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia, but you are aware that retired JNA generals established that party; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that in general terms, Your Honour. I would not be able to provide any names of retired JNA generals who established that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does the name of Admiral Branko Mamula mean anything to you? He was the Minister of Defence before Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it does, Your Honour, and I also remember now the acronym for the party. I think it was the SKPJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia, that is, do you know that these generals were hard-line communists who wanted to preserve the communist system in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is outside the scope of my report, and I remember, in general terms, what the SKPJ was supposed to -- the goals the SKPJ was pursuing, but I would not be able to provide an answer to this more detailed question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That should have been covered in your report, because you speak of the total military organisation of Yugoslavia and the Serbian people in this war, the overall organisation. You include everything; the JNA, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Srpska Krajina, the volunteer units, paramilitary organisations, and yet you leave out the most important element, the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia. Do you know that the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia, had its biggest stronghold in the security service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who was the chief of the security service of the JNA in 1990, 1991 and up to 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we talk about the Security Administration of the SFRY Armed Forces, then the name is Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Do you know that the Security Administration developed a plan to topple the leadership both in Croatia and in Slovenia and in Serbia as well, and for the army to take power in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen general information in press reports on that topic. I haven't been able to find, for example, original documents or firsthand reporting on those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the security service of the JNA was much stronger and more dangerous within Yugoslavia than the civil State Security Service and even took over much of its work?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not familiar with that. I know that on the civilian side, there was such accusations, as well as on the military side there were accusations of the opposite, especially when Mr. Milosevic -- after Mr. Milosevic became president of the Republic of Serbia, but again that's based on press reporting, secondary or third-hand sources. I haven't seen any firsthand reporting on these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You, as an officer of the Belgian Army, know full well what special psychological warfare is, do you not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm familiar with the concept of psychological operations, which is nowadays also known as information operations, but it's not conducted, at least in the armed forces of NATO countries, by intelligence service. They may provide assistance, for example, in assessing the target audience, but it is other services who are responsible for conducting such operations. But -- and just to finalise, I know from the doctrine that within the JNA it was the Security Administration who was responsible for conducting psychological operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You ought to know what a trigger event is in Western military terminology. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The military regulations and doctrine and documents I've consulted, I don't remember seeing the use of the term "trigger event."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't know that either, then. Do you know that -- well, if you're not familiar with the term, you probably don't know anything about the way it's applied. But do you know that the security service of the JNA organised the planting of explosives in the building of the Jewish community in Zagreb in order to have the explosion ascribed to Tudjman and his regime?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
