utterances.text: Your Honours, I have seen press reports on the alleged role of the -- of officials of the Security Administration of the SFRY Armed Forces in such attacks, and I believe that there was also a reference to an operation which was known under the -- or an alleged operation known under the name "Labrador," but I haven't seen any firsthand documents or sources or, yeah, information from the official organs on these events which would allow me to confirm whether the press reports are correct or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Apart from the Labrador affair, have you heard of the Opera affair?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, there was a lot of press reporting, especially in Slovene and Croatian press, on these two alleged affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the security service of the JNA organised the planting of explosives in the Jewish cemetery in Zagreb, in the Mirogoj Cemetery, the Jewish part of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript. Your Honours, I would provide the same answers I did before. I have seen reports on these alleged attacks in the media. There was a lot of attention for those things in various media, but that's all I can say. I never looked into it, I never saw any official documents or other firsthand-source information on these alleged events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that the security service of the JNA, by these explosions in Zagreb, tried to additionally compromise Tudjman as anti-semitic because his anti-semitic statements were well known from before and this was just supposed to be icing on the cake; is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to give the impression that I want to correct Mr. Seselj, but I believe the correct name is the Security Administration of the SFRY Armed Forces, just to avoid misunderstandings in the transcript, but to answer the question, I have no additional information as to what I've seen in press reports at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that security service of the JNA, or the Security Administration, it all comes to the same thing, artificially produced crimes on the Serbian side also in order to compromise Serbian nationalism, for example, in the same way that they tried to compromise Croatian nationalism by explosions in the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I haven't seen such reports. I have seen reports on crimes by forces operating under JNA control in the area of Skabrnja and Nadin, and these reports were compiled by security organs of the JNA units in the area, and they were actually corroborated by reports of other JNA units or officers, so -- which indicated actually that the events described in the reports of the security organs did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic brought the paramilitary unit called the White Eagles to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic stole several million German marks from the Vukovar Bank after the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've heard Mr. Seselj utter that accusation at several occasions. I know that Aleksandar Vasiljevic spent some time in prison in 1992, but to the best of my recollection, I don't think he was ever convicted for this alleged crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that this vast amount of money went missing from the Vukovar Bank?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen conflicting reports on that issue, because I seem to remember one report where it was said that money went to -- yeah, to the appropriate authority within the SFRY, and as Mr. Seselj claims, there were also reports that indicate that the money did not end up where it should have ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a military expert, you ought to know where that money was supposed to end up. If it's war booty, where ought to have General Vasiljevic handed in that money? You're the military expert, not me. I'm just a stupid politician who knows nothing.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what happened or did not happen with money that was allegedly found in Vukovar is outside the scope of my report. I -- while studying the role of SRS/SCP volunteers in Vukovar during the relevant time period, I did not come across information that linked these volunteers to the money that was allegedly taken from Vukovar or any other information in relation to that money that was allegedly in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you now mentioning volunteers in connection with that money? Volunteers didn't steal money anywhere. It was -- well, these volunteers were honourable men, following my model. You are a military expert who studied the JNA and the TO in depth in the former Yugoslavia, you were an expert witness in other cases, Martic and the Vukovar Troika. So as an expert, you ought to know the following: When, in armed fighting, an army takes money, any money belonging to the opposing side, where must the security officer in charge hand over that money, according to military regulations? You've studied all the military regulations, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm familiar with, in general terms, with the procedures that apply to the collection of war booty, which means that war booty has to be registered and then has to be stored and guarded. And following the -- once the conflict is ended, and we talk, for example, in that context also of the exchange of prisoners, certain measures can be applied to, for example, hand back certain parts of war booty, in particular when we talk about a significant amount of money. But those are just general principles, and I would not be able to refer to a specific SFRY Armed Forces regulation in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to the then valid regulations, the money ought to have been handed over to the military service of the National Bank. Have you ever heard of the existence of an institution called the Military Service of the National Bank of Yugoslavia? This is a trap. Beware. Don't immediately say "yes."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer I wanted to give was "no," but maybe I have to say something else now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't hear; right. Well, you didn't hear of it; right. It seems to me that I appear to be a better military expert than you, at least when it comes to the Yugoslav and Serb armies. The money was never handed over to the Military Service of the National Bank. Now, do you know that Vasiljevic was in Vukovar at the time Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I know that Vasiljevic visited Vukovar sometimes around the 18th or the 19th of November. 1991, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that General Vasiljevic personally issued orders that 200 Croatian prisoners be handed over to the civilian authorities in Eastern Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours -- I'm sorry for the transcript. No, Your Honours. On the contrary, based on the information I saw while working on the Vukovar trial, the circumstances for the hand-over of the 200 Croatian prisoners, or even more than 200, did not involve General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you were an expert witness in the Vukovar Troika trial, tell me who, by name and surname, ordered that 200 civilians be handed over -- or rather 200 prisoners, they weren't civilians, prisoners, they were prisoners of war, to hand them over to the civilian authorities, who issued that order? It wasn't established during the Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic trial. The judgement was passed, but that remained unknown. So who ordered that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to refer to the doctrine when answering that questions -- that question. The 1988 SFRY Armed Forces regulations on the application of the International Laws of War by the SFRY Armed Forces, and actually they state the same as the Geneva Conventions, state that prisoners of war are under the powers of -- under the control of the detaining power. They are not under the control of an individual, a military commander or any other officer, but of the country that has taken these people prisoner of war. And I think that is sufficient in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those prisoners of war, Mr. Theunens, did not go to Ovcara themselves of their own free will. Ovcara was not a place provided for to accommodate prisoners of war; isn't that right? The prisoners of war had to be transported to the state prison in Sremska Mitrovica, and one wing was set aside for that purpose; am I right there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There are at least three different questions on this one; how did the prisoners move around, should they have been taken to a specific prison, was capacity set aside in the prison to accommodate the prisoners. If the accused wants to go into these details with this witness, he has to put one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please try to put your question in such a way that you obtain one answer, because if you ask your question in such a way that the witness has to give four answers, then the witness, as well as the Judges, may get lost.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, this witness came here quite disoriented. We could see that today. I can't add to this state of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA took all prisoners of war from Vukovar to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, they were sent there; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that orders had been given to do so. Now, to what extent these orders were implemented is another question. In addition to Ovcara, Ovcara had been used as a transit area for both prisoners of war as well as women who were evacuated from Vukovar during the previous days. Another question was about Sremska Mitrovica. Indeed, for example, the members of the so-called -- or the Mitnica Battalion, the ZNG Mitnica Battalion. The ZNG, who surrendered on the 18th, they spent the night of 18th and 19th in Ovcara and then were escorted as prisoners of war to Sremska Mitrovica. On the 19th and 20th, a group of people who were to be evacuated from Vukovar spent the night at Ovcara, guarded by the JNA. And then on the 20th, in the afternoon, more than 200 patients of the hospital of Vukovar were escorted by members of the Guards Motorised Brigade, as well as a few members of the local Serb TO, to Ovcara, where they were handed over to members of the local Serb TO, including members of the Leva Supoderica Volunteer Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why were these prisoners of war handed over to the Territorial Defence, which had always been separated from the Guards Brigade? That's the key question. Who issued that order? Who ordered that? If all the POWs were to go to Sremska Mitrovica, who then ordered that 200 of them were to be separated and handed over to those territorials, who ordered that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I mentioned earlier, the prisoners of war were under the control at that time of what remained of SFRY, which means, in practice, they were under the control of General -- at that time Colonel Mrksic, who was in command of OG South. It was his unit that had taken the prisoners from the hospital. It was his unit that was to bring the prisoners from the hospital to Sremska Mitrovica, i.e., to implement the evacuation agreement that had been signed before in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you're a member of the OTP, why is it that the OTP didn't bring forward General Aleksandar Vasiljevic as a witness of the Prosecution in the trial of the Vukovar Troika? He appeared in the Milosevic trial. Why didn't they call him to testify in the Vukovar Troika trial, when he was in Vukovar during the liberation and when the prisoners were executed? Answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's an irrelevant question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is it not relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's not relevant to any facts in this case, why -- whether a certain witness was called or why the witness wasn't called. And I'm not even sure that the witness can actually answer the question as to why the decision was taken not to call the witness, but that's a different thing. But it's irrelevant to the factual determination of this case, why a certain witness isn't called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, regarding the fact that Aleksandar Vasiljevic was not called to witness in the so-called Vukovar trial, to testify in the Vukovar trial, is not among -- is not for you to answer, as the Prosecutor just said, but you're a member of the Prosecution here, and this case has existed, the so-called Vukovar case. The case gave rise to a judgement, but this Chamber has discussed this case in depth, so we are concerned by this case. How, then, can such a major character, I mean Vasiljevic, didn't testify? And I continue my question. Apparently his name is not on the witness list. I don't know whether he's alive or not. I really don't know. But this is the kind of questions that we have. As a military analyst, do you have an opinion about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just add, he's alive, he couldn't be more alive, and he's trembling that he might be -- might have to be held accountable for some crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he's alive. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, even though I was a member of the Prosecution team in the Vukovar investigation and the Vukovar trial, it was not me who decided about which witnesses were to be called, when, and how and so on. And so I think the best person to ask that question is Mr. Douglas Max Moore, who was a senior trial attorney in that case. I would also like to draw the honourable Judges' attention to the fact that, well, if the OTP didn't call Mr. Vasiljevic, he could have been called by the Defence if he was such an important person, he could have even been called by the Chamber, but nobody called Mr. Vasiljevic. The only thing I remember from the trial is that at one moment in time, one of the Defence attorneys came with this kind of conspiracy theory to blame Vasiljevic of the crimes in Ovcara, whereas, well, he was not called as a witness, and he could have still been called by the Defence. Looking -- from purely viewing the military documents, especially, I mean, the documents in relation to the activities of OG South, its existence, its structure, and especially its relation with the local Serb TO including Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora Detachment on the 20th of November, I didn't see any information or any other -- any information indicating a role whatsoever for Mr. Vasiljevic or General Vasiljevic in the events that led up to the killing or execution of 200 -- of over 200 people in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that my closest colleague from the JCE, the joint criminal enterprise, General Veljko Kadijevic, lives in Moscow and that he's been given political asylum in Russia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that Mr. Kadijevic now lives in Russia, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that General Kadijevic recently gave an extensive interview to Belgrade Television?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the interview, Your Honours, and I think it has to do with a new book Kadijevic published, but I haven't -- I'm not familiar with the contents of the interview, nor of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that in that interview, General Kadijevic and the whole of the Serb public was able to see that, and the Croatia and Muslim public, for that matter, that he said that General Vasiljevic, as the head of the Security Administration, did not inform him that in Ovcara a crime had been committed against prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the interview, but taking into account the position that Kadijevic held in 1991 and 1992, it would be rather surprising if Kadijevic has to wait until 2007 or 2008 in order to announce or to complain that his subordinates, including Vasiljevic, allegedly did not inform him of the crime at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question on my behalf. General Kadijevic, who resides in Moscow today and writes books and answers television interviews, apparently his name is mentioned in the indictment as a member of the joint criminal enterprise, on an equal footing -- yes, his name is there. I've just checked. We find the names of Milosevic, Kadijevic, Adzic, Mladic, Stanisic, Simatovic, Stojisic, Martic, Adzic, Karadzic, Krstic, Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Arkan, who is no longer alive today. As far as you know, is there an indictment against him, against Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the question an indictment against Kadijevic, Your Honours, or Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kadijevic, correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of an indictment against Mr. Kadijevic. I am aware that at the time, I believe an investigation was started, but I don't know what the follow-up of that investigation was, but at this time there is no indictment against Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis or Mr. Marcussen, there is an indictment mentioning the names of a number of people. Some of these people have been judged, others are fugitives. And then we come to the name of Kadijevic, who is alive. There has been no indictment against him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, might I say that it's even more of an important question, why an indictment was raised against Aleksandar Vasiljevic, although he was the head of the administration for security in the JNA throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Expert, you do not have to answer. Anyway, I see Mr. Marcussen on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is irrelevant to this case, and there are issues of prosecutorial discretion involving these sort of things that this witness can't answer, but it has nothing to do with the facts of this case, I respectfully submit, and we shouldn't go into it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "why an indictment was not raised against."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you still have five minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Theunens, that General Vasiljevic was arrested in 1992 and that he was imprisoned for a time, and that he was liberated in a strange way and pensioned off, and then he was reactivated in 1999. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I would not be able to corroborate or explain the information given by Mr. Seselj said Kadijevic was "liberated in a strange way," because I don't know the circumstances of his -- the ending of his time in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not Kadijevic, Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it was proved that he had committed great crimes and planted great crimes on others, and then he managed to escape prison, so that's obvious, because as the chief of the Security Administration, which covered the whole of Yugoslavia in terms of intelligence and counter-intelligence, he had dossiers on all the more important personages and could blackmail anyone. I know that's evident, isn't it, obvious. Just can't blackmail me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have to object to this. This is irrelevant to the case again, and making these sort of allegations against people who are not on trial here is utterly inappropriate and should not be allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Expert, General Vasiljevic is alleged to have been imprisoned in 1992. Are you aware of this, of his being in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, he was in prison in Serbia after having been put on trial there, and then at one moment in time he was released. He was pensioned off, together with a large number of other JNA officers. And then in 1999, during the NATO Kosovo bombing campaign, he was reactivated in a senior position, I think acting head of the Military Security Service, and the activation order was signed by Mr. Milosevic, who was then president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that he had been tried. In other words, he was acquitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact details, Your Honours. I've seen one press article which stated that none of the charges could be proven, but I'm not sure to what extent that article is correct. I don't know whether he was acquitted, but he was released quite early, that's what I remember, quite soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, as we're coming to the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of that, I'd like to make a comment or objection, Mr. President. I think that this is highly symptomatic, that is to say, that the Prosecution wasn't interested at all in the case of General Vasiljevic, they weren't interested in that, however they cooperate very successfully with him in fabricating false documents. So I'm sure that the OTP would have had to have been interested in the Belgrade trial of General Vasiljevic and to have -- come by all the documents and be well informed on the subject. I was president of the Serbian Radical Party at the time with just one member of Parliament, and they're taking me to task for that, whereas they are completely ignoring the head of the security of the JNA who was involved in everything, many crimes he perpetrated for political reasons in order to topple the regime and Belgrade and Zagreb, and the Prosecution seems to be uninterested in all that. So I think the Trial Chamber should instruct the Prosecution to gather all the documents related to the General Vasiljevic trial, because my associates cannot come by those documents in Belgrade; they come up against a wall when they try to do so, and pursuant to Rule 68, it would be valuable material, as far as I'm concerned, for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In view of this request by the accused, I'm asking the OTP whether you have a copy of the sentence that was given at the end -- when General Vasiljevic was acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will have to look, Your Honours. I do maintain the position that these things are irrelevant, and it is inappropriate for the accused to make these sort of allegations. With this particular witness, there's no problem. With the previous witnesses that have been here, there's no problem, but it sends out a message that witnesses who are going to come here are going to be bullied, and we should maintain a proper decorum in court so we can proceed with this case in a proper manner where witnesses can come and give their evidence in future under proper conditions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just ten seconds, please, Mr. President, just ten seconds of the time. General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, in the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic, is quoted as one of the members of the joint criminal enterprise, and he is not in my indictment. Now, the person who wrote that knew full well that Slobodan Milosevic, in the cross-examination, would spare him the most difficult questions, and he knew that in my trial, I would not take care of Vasiljevic's feelings at all, and that's why he's not among the JCE in my indictment, whereas he was in the indictment against Milosevic. I would certainly not spare him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I'm going to check on this. It is 10 to 2.00. Tomorrow we resume at 8.30 a.m. Mr. Seselj, you're probably left with a little more than an hour. I'll tell you tomorrow. So tomorrow at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of February, 2008, at 8.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
